Business.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
Business.text:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

But tech stocks more broadly also fell.

Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

Business.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervenes
Business.text:
Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after Donald Trump directly intervened with the US AI chipmaker’s board of directors, in a stunning reversal of the tech billionaire’s downfall.

Speaking on Monday shortly after Nvidia’s surprise announcement that Huang had been restored to the top job – less than two weeks after he resigned – Trump said he had “convinced” the board to do it. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC. Huang had resigned after reports of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees.

“It’s very exciting news. I felt very strongly that he should come back,” the US president said.

Huang said he was “honored to return to Nvidia” and lead “one of the most consequential technology companies in the world”. He added: “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

Nvidia shares surged on the news of Huang’s return, jumping 32% and adding more than $1tn (£760bn) to the company’s market value in New York on Monday, while Trump, who had persistently called for Huang’s return, said: “The country needs Jensen’s leadership.”

The chipmaker’s move to bring Huang back marks a sharp reversal from its board’s decision days earlier to rule out his return. The US vice-president, JD Vance, played a key role in discussions between the White House, Huang and Nvidia, according to the New York Times.

The US government has been investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company formerly run by Huang’s alleged former lover, Alice Huang (no relation), over suspected diversion of semiconductors in breach of export controls, amid concerns Nvidia’s powerful AI chips may have been smuggled into China. Alice Huang has also been named in multiple reports as a Chinese spy.

The same day as Huang’s reinstatement, the US government announced it had added Megaspeed to a federal trade blacklist, preventing US companies from selling chips or other advanced technology to the Singaporean business.

Trump said on Monday that the US government had “no evidence that [Jensen Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct” and that the attorney general, Todd Blanche, felt Huang was “exonerated”.

The US president told CNBC that the US had to “protect our geniuses”, adding that the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, praised Huang at last week’s Apec summit in Shenzhen. Adding that he had talked to Nvidia’s directors, he said: “I’ve been speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it. I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company.”

Nvidia’s share price had fallen by a quarter in the days after Huang resigned on 12 November. The falls were mirrored by a wider AI rout in global stock markets last week as investors feared new leadership at Nvidia could dampen prospects for AI companies that rely on the company’s chips to develop and operate AI tools such as chatbots, as well as having close financial ties with the chipmaker.

News of his shock reinstatement sparked a wider rally not just in Nvidia’s shares but on Wall Street as a whole, sending the Nasdaq composite index up 6.5% and the S&P 500 by 4.7%. The US dollar was lifted to a 19-month high.

In a statement, Nvidia said its board of directors had talked to Huang and were “satisfied with respect to Mr Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia”. Nvidia added that it had received input from “senior levels” of the US government and was confident his reinstatement “poses no national security risk”.

A senior Democrat, Elizabeth Warren, a senator for Massachusetts, said the decision was “reckless”, adding that it did not change the fact that Huang owed Congress answers about Nvidia’s compliance with trade restrictions on its powerful AI chips. He is due to give evidence to Congress on 1 December. The state of California is also investigating whether Nvidia’s advanced chips ended up in China in violation of US restrictions.

She said his return increased the urgency of Congress passing export control bills “and making sure that Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk”.

Nvidia said an independent investigation into allegations Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation was ongoing and “will proceed to conclusion”.

Harvey Jones, the Nvidia chair, who was appointed this month after Huang’s resignation, said: “The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

Huang built Nvidia from a video-game chip designer into the dominant supplier of AI processors, steering its roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties along the way. He resigned after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for China, an allegation Beijing denies. It was also reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with two other Nvidia employees.

Trump praised Nvidia’s board for making “the correct and proper decision” and posted: “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”

It came hours after reports that Alice Huang had been in contact with an official in China’s spy agency while she was having an affair with the Nvidia boss. People with knowledge of US intelligence reports claimed she was in touch with the Chinese official until this autumn, according to the New York Times.

The Arm Holdings chief executive, Rene Haas, who had been approached to succeed Huang, has signed a new deal that will keep him in his current role until 2033. Huang had been replaced on a temporary basis by Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief.

Elon Musk, who had called for Huang to return in an open letter backed by other Silicon Valley heavyweights, posted on X: “Welcome back the main man,” alongside a picture of him shaking hands with Huang. Trump said he had spoken to Musk “over the last week or so” about the Huang situation.

Sam North, a market analyst at the trading platform eToro, said: “Jensen Huang’s return underlines how much of the AI trade still rests on one man.”

Huang’s reinstatement has echoes of another recent real-life Silicon Valley drama. His return has taken place almost three years to the day since OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, brought back its chief executive, Sam Altman, after a similar bout of turmoil. Altman was removed by his board on 17 November 2023 but was restored five days later following an internal power battle.

In a post on X on Monday Altman wrote: “Jensen!”

Business.title: Wild stock market swings: will I lose money, and is there anything I can do?
Business.text:
Will I lose money?

Lots of people own shares that are falling in value, either through their pension or other type of investment account. Many of the shares that are experiencing the biggest falls are companies that have dominated indices and, as a result, the passive funds that track them.

Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at AJ Bell, says two of the most popular passive investments among investors are global equity funds and funds tracking the S&P 500 US stock market index. “Both have exposure to the giants of tech in a large way,” he says. And, as a result, both have fallen in recent days.

Coatsworth says that, while 15 years ago US shares represented half of the MSCI World index – a benchmark for the global stock market – it is now 73%. Tech is the dominant sector and officially represents 30% of the index. However, Google’s parent Alphabet and Facebook’s owner Meta are classed as communication services stocks – adding them bumps up tech to about 35% of the index.

Investors who think they have diversified by being in a global fund may be having a nasty surprise.

The investment platform interactive investor (ii) reports on the top holdings of its customers every quarter. Its most recent report shows global tracker funds are well-represented in their portfolios, as is Scottish Mortgage – an actively managed investment trust that holds shares in SpaceX, Nvidia and Anthropic, among others.

However, an important thing to remember about falling share prices is that you do not lose money until you sell. Only at that point do you crystallise your loss.

And you may not even have losses on paper, depending on when you invested. In recent years stock markets have been climbing. The FTSE 100 is still higher than it was last year. Scottish Mortgage has been falling since mid-October, but its shares are still well up on this time last year.

How do I diversify to avoid further tech downturns?

Coatsworth says there are a few paths to consider.

“One way to dial down tech exposure is to switch into a global equity fund that excludes the US,” he says. “For example, iShares MSCI World ex-US ETF invests in a basket of companies from around the world excluding the US.”

Tech stocks outside the US account for 10.9% of the portfolio, but the main holdings include banks, healthcare companies, oil producers and miners. “That would provide more sector balance and less dependence on tech, but it would mean some of the key names that have led the US market rally in recent years like Nvidia no longer being in the driving seat,” he says. However, if those stocks recover, you will be missing out on any potential gains.

He says a possible “middle ground” is the Invesco MSCI World Equal Weight ETF. At the end of September, the US represented 40.6% of the investment – less than with a traditional global equity fund. “The investor still has their toe in the pond for US tech exposure, but they wouldn’t be up to their neck in the water,” he says.

Business.title: Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says
Business.text:
Invoking Greek mythology, the US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, by which the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union, the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders were either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

“And if Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Business.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
Business.text:
Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11.

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage. She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.

“I presumed there had been a hack of the aviation system and that it would be down for days,” she said.

Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.”

This was not an isolated view. What happened in the days after the incident, which began on Thursday 12 November, left many wondering if the US, and the western world, was under a coordinated assault. By Tuesday big US banks, Apple, and the National Security Agency had also been affected by technical glitches. Researchers also flagged a cyber-attack that targeted 178 organisations worldwide, although the financial losses appeared to be small.

The truth is more prosaic. The chaos of the previous weeks – grounded planes, frozen email servers, iPhone outages – appears, on closer examination, to be more a string of coincidences than anything else, in part driven by fears over advancing artificial intelligence.

But the narratives that have sprung up around it are a measure of an unstable and frenetic global mood, which is dealing with two powerful trends: the rot of decades-old infrastructure from chronic underinvestment and the genesis of some of the most powerful technology humanity has made – AI.

The failure that delayed Reindorf’s takeoff originated with a faulty router in the city of El Dorado, Arkansas, population 16,609.

That router was installed in the midst of a maintenance procedure that has been under way for more than two decades. In 2002, the US government contracted a small company, now known as L3Harris, to modernise the communications system of the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA), in charge of America’s airports. As a part of it, L3Harris has been tearing up communication lines made of copper wire across the country, and replacing them with fibre optic cables.

This glacial undertaking sparked a sudden and unprecedented catastrophe – the router, newly replaced, misfired and caused air traffic communications across the US to crash, bringing all departing flights nationwide to a grinding halt. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled.

L3Harris’s contracts, which have now run into the billions of dollars, are one emblem of where the world is today: mired in ageing infrastructure that is slowly failing, yet immensely costly to replace.

There is a broad sense that governments everywhere are not equipped to deal with this. In the US, oversight reports have been urgently calling for upgrades to the FAA for years. The FAA only announced that it would phase out the use of decades-old floppy discs containing vital weather and other critical information just last year.

Meanwhile, there are more subtle issues around other incidents, such as the Microsoft outage. An upgrade in July left in place a software bug that lurked quietly for months before a string of coincidences triggered it – overwhelming the company’s servers and halting the use of most of Microsoft’s systems worldwide. The outage halted everyday procedures such as the release of detainees in American jails and access to some patients records at UK hospitals.

It was accompanied by more chaos. A software bug at JP Morgan Chase, the largest bank in the US, delayed transactions, a disruption that rippled throughout the country’s banks and their customers. An internal update at Apple caused outages of some of its iPhone apps. Routine maintenance went awry at the US Department of Defense’s National Security Agency (NSA), temporarily disrupting the internal network the agency uses to send and receive classified information.

Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and Apple might have moved far beyond copper wire and floppy discs, mostly, but they – and software companies everywhere – have been forced to run at double the pace in recent months, because of a deluge of bugs being discovered by AI. This might not be the specific reason for those upgrades; some maintenance is routine.

But AI-driven hacking has ushered in a new reality for IT professionals. The NSA told Congress that its communication outage was a result of quick fixes to systems identified as vulnerable by AI.

To recap: this spring, Anthropic and OpenAI both released powerful AI models capable of finding bugs in lines of code. They immediately spun this to the media, suggesting that all software, everywhere, is extraordinarily vulnerable to AI-driven hacking – and offering their tools to banks and spying agencies.

Some have argued that this hype is not entirely justified, suggesting that many vulnerabilities these models discover are not particularly useful to hackers. But the threat of AI-driven hacking has changed the game.

One senior cybersecurity professional told the Guardian the relentless exposure of IT flaws had left their team “exhausted”.

AI helped to uncover a bug in the PHP programming language in October. This was followed by the discovery of a vulnerability in the Java programming language on Tuesday, followed by another bug in NGINX, a web server.

“When NGINX happened I thought, ‘Oh come on – another one?’,” said the professional.

Java and PHP are both part of the essential backbone of the internet, vital infrastructure that keeps most of the world online.

“AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery so rapidly that organisations are applying patches at a volume and pace their systems were never built to absorb,” said Jamieson O’Reilly, a cybersecurity specialist.

Tech companies are constantly finding potential bugs and fixing them. Now they have to do it a lot faster, said O’Reilly: “The volume and speed of AI-driven discovery makes their problems far more acute.”

The backdrop to all this was a cybersecurity narrative already running at a fraught pitch due to the hacks of supermarket fridges across Europe, global scares such as the discovery of the flaw in PHP and the multibillion-dollar hack of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange.

Social media filled the gaps where organisations could not immediately supply information. Laura Loomer, a prominent conspiracy peddler, posted on X that “we are clearly being attacked by foreign adversaries via cyber-attacks”, adding “go get cash”. On TikTok, there are posts about a #90daypoweroutage, a conspiracy theory sparked by a nationwide test of the US emergency alert system – and a Simpsons clip.

The consequences of conspiratorial thinking can be seen at Costco, a bulk-buying retailer, where there has been a rise in emergency prep sales including purchases of generators, and general “pantry-loading” in the UK. Analysts at Mizuho Bank said this was a result of “consumer anxiety” following the outages and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media”.

These concerns have not been confined to the fringes. The UK government recently told its citizens to stock up on three days’ worth of cash, among other basic items, as part of a readiness-for-crisis campaign.

Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, whose research centres on the spread of myths and misinformation, said the “clustering” of events such as multiple outages “can be perceived as being indicative of purposeful coordination rather than chance”.

Feeding into the anxiety, there have also been examples of state and criminal actors causing disruption, from Russia targeting undersea internet cables to last year’s crippling of Britain’s biggest carmaker, Jaguar Land Rover, which give credence to public concerns. A solution, said Lewandowsky, was “for responsible governments to be transparent and accurate in their communications” in order to suppress wilder explanations.

Taken together, experts say that the string of outages highlights the stunning fragility of US and global infrastructure, where a single mistake or malfunction can bring entire transportation, communication, and security systems to a standstill.

“We’ve built a world in which essential systems are so interconnected that a failure in one can just cascade through those systems really quickly,” said Aarathi Krishnan, the founder of Raksha Intelligence Futures, a global intelligence firm. “All of our systems, whether it’s comms, finance, capital, all of it, are so interconnected and concentrated, it creates a dependence. And that dependence creates fragility.”

What can be done? It is unclear. AI-driven bug discovery is not going to slow down and the legacy systems the world is grappling with are what they are. Infrastructure is the often overlooked backbone of society and those who decades ago built networks of road and air traffic systems and electrical grids could not have anticipated these modern threats.

Mike Chapple, the faculty director of Notre Dame University’s business computer science programme, said it was “unfortunate” that one faulty router could have such an effect on a nation’s aviation communication system.

“That just points to a design that isn’t resilient – it shouldn’t be designed in a way that one failure at one location can cause the whole nationwide system to come tumbling down.”

More troubling hacks, and more conspiracy theories, are probably on the horizon. The senior cybersecurity professional said heightened public awareness of cyber disruption had led to hypersensitivity about any incident.

“It’s like the tide has gone out on cybersecurity in terms of public perception, and there’s the same amount of wrecks out there as there have been for years. Any time you change a complex system, stuff happens.”

However, the professional is concerned that AI, with its capacity to identify flaws, help plan attacks and execute them, will be harnessed by “already very competent” adversaries. Referring to the general state of IT security around the world, the source added: “Thank goodness we haven’t had an AI-sourced vulnerability that is easy to exploit. Because that would be carnage.”

For many, though, recent events have been bad enough.

When Josephine’s* prescription request for lithium for her bipolar disorder was lost “in the ether” during the global Microsoft outage, she admits she was “freaking out”.

“My medication is life-changing and keeps me stable,” said the 26-year-old, a student living in the east of England. After an agonising wait, she was finally able to collect her prescription, but the experience has left her deeply troubled.

“For myself and many others, we struggled to access life-saving medication,” she said. “It is alarming there was no contingency plan.”

* Name has been changed

Additional reporting by Jane Clinton

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage. She immediately suspected the two...

Sports.title: Fifa presidential race: Gianni Infantino private-jet flights under scrutiny
Sports.text:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino's globetrotting by private jet since his plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup can be revealed.

BBC Sport found Infantino has taken 39 private flights - the equivalent of one every three days - and visited 32 different countries since the news emerged on 28 July.

Our research found he travelled more than 102,800 air miles and spent just under nine days in the air in the space of 115 days.

Critics have accused of Infantino of using tools only at his disposal as president to aid his campaign for re-election next March.

They questioned whether his re-election campaign may have partly motivated any promises made or support offered during those visits.

Fifa said Infantino had a "statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations".

However, he visited nearly double the 18 countries he did in the same period in 2025.

The initial Times story that revealed Infantino's World Cup plan led to a wave of criticism around the world.

But, as BBC Sport revealed, many observers feel Infantino is now the favourite to be re-elected in the spring after his rivals struggled to find a candidate to run against him until the last moment.

And it appears Infantino has managed to shore up support around the world, with critics suggesting his globetrotting was a key part of that strategy.

There has also been concern about the environmental impact of his extensive travels.

Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - said Infantino's travelling was "part of his campaign".

He told BBC Sport: "The issue here is that Fifa does not have rules on campaign funding, so the president can claim that he's going there on official business when indirectly he's using that to campaign.

"And anyone else running against him very likely will not have the financial means to compete with that."

Infantino's position seemed vulnerable after it emerged he had been devising a plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, in a proposal called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

Before FFE was abandoned, Infantino wrote to all 211 member associations saying they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed the plan.

Lars-Christer Olsson - a former chief executive of Uefa - told BBC Sport the "important" question was "what does he promise and what are the conditions, as he already did when he promised cash if the members supported his FFE project?"

BBC Sport gleaned the information about where Infantino had been travelling to, and when, from postings on his social media accounts.

The reasons for his travels include holding meetings with football association presidents, opening pitches, meeting politicians and attending confederation gatherings.

The private jets he used are operated by Qatar Executive (QE) - a subsidiary of the Qatar Airways Group, which is one of Fifa's sponsors.

BBC Sport used flight-tracking records and the jet registrations of the Qatar Executive fleet to compile a detailed log of Infantino's flights, totalling at least 39 since the start of August. Fifa did not dispute the figure.

It said "all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations" and there are "rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official".

But Fifa declined to comment on how the use of QE flights impacts on the money available from the Qatar Airways sponsorship for the benefit of global football.

The governing body also declined to comment when asked when Infantino had last taken a commercial flight.

Olsson said: "What do these trips cost and who is paying, which are the implications for the total football community?

"Is he provided with transport in his private campaign with the idea of getting something back in return if he is elected? If Fifa is paying for private jets, would it not be better to invest this money in the member associations?"

Maduro said: "That's again a confusion between his role as president of Fifa and his role as candidate to Fifa presidency."

He said there were no regulations within Fifa on the "use of public money to support their campaign".

"There's no independent authority that controls that, there is no regulation of campaign funding," he said.

Infantino's trips included attending the Caribbean Football Union presidents' meeting and a junior football tournament in the Dominican Republic three weeks after FFE failed.

He then flew to Paris, where he attended the esports World Cup , alongside French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman.

On his Instagram account, Infantino said he had "pledged Fifa's support" for the Pakistan Football Federation president's development plans when he met him in the US in September.

A few days later, he referenced a "wonderful discussion" with the president of the Latvian Football Federation during a visit to Riga, describing him as "my dear friend".

During a visit to Indonesia in October for the final of the Fifa ASEAN Cup, he met presidents from the football federations of Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, Maldives, Mongolia, Myanmar, Pakistan, Philippines, Qatar, Singapore, Thailand and Timor-Leste.

He said: "Having your support and shared passion on this momentous occasion means a great deal and together we will continue driving this game forward."

And during a recent trip to Manila, he performed on stage as part of a quartet called the 'Backache Boys', alongside officials from the Asian Football Confederation, and the football federations of Malaysia and the Philippines.

A spokesperson for Fifa said its objectives were to "improve football constantly and promote it globally".

They added: "The Fifa president has a statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations.

"To do that, he travels around the world and attends Fifa's tournaments and events. Mr Infantino is elected until 18 March 2027, when the next Fifa presidential election will take place.

"Fifa has put in place rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official.

"The Fifa president routinely travels around the world for various duties, together with relevant officials, on business and tournament-related matters and strives to visit member associations of Fifa whenever he can.

"Fifa expenses are published in our annual report, and all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations.

"Fifa's money belongs to the 211 member associations and an increased investment to $6.35bn for the upcoming cycle reinforces our unwavering commitment to further supporting football development and access globally."

Sports.title: Kevin de Bruyne: Why has midfielder struggled at Napoli ahead of Man City return?
Sports.text:
Kevin de Bruyne's move to Napoli in 2025 was supposed to mark a continuation of his glittering decade at Manchester City as he approaches the twilight years of his career.

Instead, the midfielder, who is widely regarded as one of the stand-out players of his generation, has seen his time in Naples threaten to turn sour amid an early injury, friction with his team-mates and rumours of a January exit.

Napoli were Serie A champions in 2024-25 - the year before De Bruyne's arrival - but are currently languishing in eighth, while they sit 27th in the Champions League after a heavy 4-1 defeat at Porto earlier this month.

Belgium international De Bruyne lifted 16 trophies in his 10 years at City and is guaranteed a generous ovation when he returns to the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday but the highs of his time in England are in contrast to the struggles he is seemingly enduring in Italy.

"Not a lot I can say for the moment," said De Bruyne when asked about his future. "I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

"There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening."

City decided not to renew De Bruyne's contract during the 2024-25 season and the player had the choice of heading to the US with Chicago Fire or staying in one of the top-five leagues in Europe.

The 35-year-old felt he could still cut it at the highest level but his first season at Napoli was heavily disrupted by a hamstring injury which kept him out for more than four months, restricting him to 21 appearances.

Napoli finished runners up to Inter Milan to lose their Serie A title and De Bruyne reportedly said, external he was "happy" manager Antonio Conte had departed in the summer as promises were not kept regarding the style of play.

But despite making his name as a technically gifted number 10, De Bruyne's role has been remodelled into a deeper holding one under Massimiliano Allegri in an ageing squad that has struggled this season.

In Porto, the fractures were clear to see, with De Bruyne having a heated on-field confrontation, external with striker Lorenzo Lucca and his team-mates were forced to step in to diffuse the situation.

The passionate side of De Bruyne's game was shown in Manchester too.

The midfielder shouted "shut up" at manager Pep Guardiola during a Champions League game against Real Madrid in 2023, and said "let me talk" when David Silva and Fernandinho were ushering him off the pitch at half-time shortly after he was booked against Napoli in 2017.

"Speaking about the pitch, De Bruyne is the best player this year at Napoli," Naples-based journalist Vincenzo Credendino tells BBC Sport. "The point is that the whole team is having difficulties.

"We saw that there is a problem, at least between De Bruyne and Lorenzo Lucca. Their acting was very, very clear and I think that in that time, the two of them were wrong.

"On one hand you cannot swear at another team-mate but on the other hand, De Bruyne reproached Lucca without encouraging him, so it was a bad show."

De Bruyne has played 16 times for Napoli this season - contributing four goals and two assists - but his long-term future at the club remains unclear.

In September, De Bruyne's wife reportedly, external told a Belgian publication about their desire to move back home, saying "the sooner we get there, the better" as the player leads a "very restricted life" in Naples.

Asked if the quotes had been misinterpreted, De Bruyne said: "To be honest, I am pretty annoyed because if you read the article, that none of you have read, to understand what she said.

"I was away in Belgium and a lot of noise came and a lot of bad reactions to my wife and family. I saw pictures of my house, I don't think it is OK but it is what it is and some press created this in Italy. I don't know why.

"Nobody knows my life, you will never know. People who work with me are not allowed to say anything but obviously it is something that I take away and think about. It has not been nice for my wife or for my family."

It has led to interest from the Netherlands with PSV Eindhoven making a £1.67m offer to sign him in January, but the two clubs are apart in their valuations as Napoli want up to £6.7m, according to Credendino.

"Napoli fans were not happy [with the interview]," he says. "There are many fans that say, 'OK, you can leave if you want, we are not putting chains on anybody'."

Napoli boss Allegri left the door open for a January exit by saying in his pre-match news conference the pair had "not spoken" about his future and it is "down to the players and who wants to leave" when the transfer window opens.

City manager Enzo Maresca was assistant to Pep Guardiola during the 2022-23 campaign in which De Bruyne helped the club to a Treble of trophies and the Italian has fond memories of the "fantastic season" they spent together.

"No doubt, [he is] one of the best," Maresca said of De Bruyne in his pre-match news conference. "Not only personally but also for the history of this club. In the last 10 years all the trophies the club achieved Kevin was here.

"He was an important player, a top guy, polite and for me it was a pleasure to work with him."

This is not the first time De Bruyne will be facing his former club with a reunion with City in the Champions League last season.

That trip turned out to be a bitterly unhappy experience, with De Bruyne substituted after 26 minutes following Giovanni di Lorenzo's red card in the 2-0 defeat.

The midfielder will be hoping for a better result on Tuesday as he aims to park his struggles for one evening.

City and Belgium winger Jeremy Doku said: "Kevin is someone that likes football. Even at this age he loves it.

"I don't have any doubts about his quality and I am sure everything will be fine in Napoli."

Sports.title: F1 Q&A: Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc, Max Verstappen and George Russell feature
Sports.text:
After Las Vegas, have Ferrari now reached a crossroads? With Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc's on-track antics, is their partnership sustainable? Should Ferrari consider a change of direction, potentially bringing Oliver Bearman into the equation? - Michael

The battle between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at Ferrari is one that keeps on giving - but not in a way Ferrari would want.

The collision in Las Vegas for which Leclerc was penalised was just the latest flashpoint for the team in a season that has been full of them.

The drivers argued over race strategy in relation to each other in Zandvoort and Singapore.

Hamilton made an aggressive dive down the inside at the first chicane on the first lap at Monza, only for Leclerc to shove him on to the gravel.

Hamilton ignored calls to pit in both Singapore (because he didn't want to just circulate behind Leclerc) and Brazil (because, he said, he had not been given enough information about the weather).

There was the first-lap incident at Turn Four in Mexico in which their fighting led to both going off track and letting in Max Verstappen to win a race Ferrari should have finished one-two.

And now Las Vegas, where first Hamilton earned a 10-second penalty for gaining a position on Lando Norris on track in an incident that also involved Leclerc, then Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for tipping Hamilton into a spin later in the race.

Leclerc was on the receiving end of team principal Frederic Vasseur's ire in Las Vegas - the Frenchman calling the situation "unacceptable". But inside Ferrari they felt both drivers had a degree of culpability for the Mexico situation.

Somehow Vasseur needs to get a handle on this.

Ferrari want to allow them to race. And it's hard to imagine two drivers of such standing would accept anything else.

The problem is that doing so, amid their battle for supremacy within the team, is harming the team's results.

The concern for Ferrari is this is happening when there is relatively little at stake. It's easy to imagine how combustible it could become if Ferrari have a car capable of challenging for the title next year.

Both want to be the driver to deliver that next championship, for very different reasons.

Hamilton would get his eighth, which he feels he was unfairly denied in Abu Dhabi in 2021. And Leclerc would win his first, and complete the journey of being the first Ferrari academy driver to win the world championship for the team.

At the moment, this is not an existential question, but it's easy to see how it could become one, and Ferrari left with a decision of it being one or the other if they can't find a way to race without compromising the team.

But that's not just on Vasseur.

Both drivers have buy into that and, as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have largely done at McLaren, accept there will be days when they have to sacrifice themselves for the greater good of Ferrari while ensuring they are ahead of the other more often than not on speed and fair racing.

It's then up to the team to decide when there comes a point to impose team orders if either or both are in a title fight with another driver.

It remains to be seen whether either of them can fully buy into that in circumstances when they individually end up losing out.

Why does George Russell often feel the need to try mind games and make comments, such as those about Max Verstappen? It often backfires on him and are usually made when he's got nothing to race for. Shouldn't he focus on himself? - Nick

This, as Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff pointed out after the race in Las Vegas, is a rivalry that goes back years.

"They've known each other so long," was Wolff's verdict. "Since karting. I think it's probably been a bit of cat and mouse. Provocations on either side. Another good factor of entertainment."

Verstappen also had a bit of a set-to with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in Mexico practice, which was not dissimilar in some ways.

There, stewards ruled that both had driven in an "unacceptable manner" and both drivers admitted their moves had been unnecessary and clumsy.

There's no question Russell believed what he was saying about Verstappen's driving in final practice at Las Vegas. According to the stewards, he was in the right, as Verstappen was given a warning for his changing direction in the braking zone.

Are these mind games? Or just Russell saying what he thinks? He feels he has a valid point to make.

Making it in public does not seem to affect Verstappen in any way. Does it change anything? Verstappen is a remorseless, ruthless competitor on track whether he is provoked or not.

Yes, he admitted satisfaction when he saw Russell make his late-race error in Las Vegas. But did he race any differently because of the Briton's comments? That's unlikely. Verstappen was just doing what he felt was right to win the race.

Ultimately, it's Russell's career, and it's up to him how he conducts himself, what he chooses to say in public and what he does not.

Track design, cold temperatures, energy deployment strategies or just the unwillingness of one team-mate to hold station behind another. What was the dominant factor in Las Vegas that led to such a hectic race? - Tim

The extraordinary Las Vegas race, with long trains of cars unable to break free of each other, was a combination of technical factors. Nothing to do with the willingness or otherwise of team-mates to hold station.

It was a combination of the track characteristics, particularly the long straights, the energy deployment demands of the engines, which are energy starved, and the cold temperatures and track surface and the effect they had on tyre behaviour.

As Max Verstappen said: "It was just the tow (in) combination with the deployment. Of course, when you are within a second, you have the overtake mode as well, and around here that is powerful. So, you could not pull away."

The tow provided a significant lap time gain of well over 0.5secs a lap. That's why a car in front could not pull away from a car behind even if it was slightly quicker.

The overtake mode provides an extra 0.5MJ of electrical energy per lap for a car following another by under a second. So that's another factor preventing someone pulling away.

Then the batteries were running out before the end of the straights, so a car running in front in free air was suffering from that, too.

On top of that, Las Vegas is a smooth track which is light on tyres. So degradation was almost non-existent. That kept tyre temperatures under control and allowed people to push hard throughout.

If the tyres had shown their usual behaviour of surface overheating leading to sliding, there would have been less action as drivers would have found it much harder to follow each other closely. As is usually the case in F1.

Drivers have been pushing for years for tyres to behave in this way, but so far Pirelli has been unable or unwilling to provide them. It only happens occasionally in specific circumstances.

The flip side of the argument is that so-called zero-deg races are sometimes boring as much as they are sometimes great, because drivers pushing to the limit can means less overtaking. Not in this case, though

With a move to engines with a smaller electrical component in 2030, are F1 cars becoming less relevant to modern road cars? The argument was always that F1 is the test bed for future road car technology. - Paul

The current F1 engines, with a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, were decided upon five or so years ago when the road-car market was slightly different to now.

The push for electrification is still there, and will continue. But consumer take-up of electric cars, especially in the performance market, has not been what manufacturers expected. Hence a slight shift in focus.

That said, it's not as if the current F1 engines are especially road relevant. With a few exceptions, road cars tend to be either full electric, plug-in hybrid, where the electrical element is much less than 50-50, or full internal combustion.

So there is an argument the new engines, with sustainable fuel and a hybrid element that is about 12-13% of total output normally or 25% when on overtake mode, are more relevant to road cars, not less, at least in their fundamental architecture.

The sustainable fuel is key here.

If this can get to a point where it is available to the mass market - and F1 is simplifying the demands on its make-up for the next ruleset in an attempt to help make the fuel more cost-effective for exactly that reason - it could be a game-changer for emissions in the road-car market.

That's because there will inevitably be a lot of legacy internal combustion vehicles on the road globally for many years, even after the new-car market becomes fully electric.

So if emissions from these can be reduced by 80%, as is the ballpark figure for the carbon-impact reduction of sustainable fuels versus fossil fuels, that's a major step.

Don't forget, too, the 2030 rules were the product of talks between the manufacturers and the FIA.

It was the manufacturers who pushed back against FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem's initial desire for a naturally aspirated engine with no hybrid element.

And they did that exactly because it made them more road relevant.

Sports.title: Viktor Gyokeres: What's going on with the Arsenal striker?
Sports.text:
A Premier League trophy and 21 goals in his debut season - on paper things have worked out perfectly for Viktor Gyokeres since his £64m transfer to Arsenal.

But, even with those achievements, it has been a tough start to the current campaign for the 28-year-old striker.

The Swede has started just one Premier League game this season and is yet to score in his eight league appearances.

He has started three games in the Champions League, two in the Carabao Cup, and has scored just twice in 15 games in all competitions. Not the numbers he would have hoped for after last season's glory.

It is not just this season that has seen Gyokeres suitability questioned for Arsenal though.

Even though he scored more than 20 goals in his first season in all competitions as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait for a title, his all-round game had its critics.

It has been near enough a straight battle for the number nine role between Kai Havertz and Gyokeres since the Swedish international signed.

And Gyokeres was thrust into leading the line for Arsenal quicker and more frequently than planned after injury kept Havertz out for long periods last season.

Although the Swede may be the more natural finisher, Havertz's all-round play is considered superior with the German also one of Arteta's most trusted players for big games.

Gyokeres, a "win-now signing", was bought for his ability to find the net but also for how he could open up spaces for his team-mates, something they have praised him for.

But playing with his back to goal and linking up play is not natural to Gyokeres and his failure to hold up the ball or win duels with centre-backs has led to fan frustration.

Arteta has spoken about how the striker has been working on improving his hold-up play and connections, and there were hints of it in the Champions League win over Slavia Prague where Gyokeres assisted the opener and scored the winner in arguably his best game of the season.

A big reason that Gyokeres is not starting games is that Havertz is fit.

Last season, Havertz suffered with knee and hamstring issues which meant Gyokeres was the only option Arteta had.

Had Havertz been fit, he would have played a lot more and the fact that he started the Champions League final and the key match away at Manchester City in last season's title race back this up.

This season Gyokeres has just six starts and Arteta says that his gametime and situation is similar to other members in the squad.

"We have rotated the team a lot and used the competitions as well to give minutes to players and exposure because they are all starters in my opinion," Arteta said.

"Viktor's case is one of many that they have been in the same situation where they play more in the Premier League or more in the Champions League which is not bad, eh?"

Arteta is open with his players about their standing in the squad and said that Gyokeres has not approached him directly about a lack of minutes.

"We have conversations with every player to make sure that they understand what we are doing and to gather information about the way we are feeling and so far it has been very positive with Viktor and the rest of the team," he said.

The signing of Gyokeres is an interesting one in its own right.

The Arsenal recruitment team had done a lot of due diligence on signing, now Manchester United forward, Benjamin Sesko.

It is understood work on that deal had been done but a change of direction to sign Gyokeres happened after Andrea Berta became Arsenal sporting director.

Some around Arsenal have always thought that Gyokeres is not the usual forward that the Gunners would go for and his predicament of a lack of game time was always likely to happen, even if he did play a big part in them ending their trophy drought.

Sports.title: Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?
Sports.text:
It had been some run for Everton captain James Tarkowski.

Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.

But that run came to an end at Brentford as he was given his first red card in his 351st Premier League appearance, although the decision has attracted plenty of debate.

His dismissal crucially means he will miss Sunday's Merseyside derby against Liverpool and also ruined David Moyes' record-breaking night as he took charge of his 593rd game as Everton boss - more than anyone else in the club's history.

The 4-0 loss was also the heaviest defeat Everton have had since Moyes returned to the club at the start of last year.

Tarkowski's dismissal proved a big talking point during and after the match, with opinions split on whether he should have gone. Even Moyes wasn't sure.

He told BBC Match of the Day: "My thoughts at the time, I didn't think it was but when I've looked at it again I think his foot is high. Is there enough force for it to be a red card? Not sure about that."

So what exactly happened?

Just 15 minutes after Keane Lewis-Potter scored his second deflected strike of the evening, Everton skipper Tarkowski thundered into a challenge on Brentford's Yehor Yarmoliuk.

He won the ball but also followed through with the challenge forcefully. Initially, referee Craig Pawson deemed a foul and a yellow card was enough.

But, after an intervention from the video assistant referee (VAR) and studying the replay, Pawson changed the yellow for a red.

The Premier League match centre said on X: "After VAR review, the referee overturned the original decision of yellow card for Tarkowski for the challenge on Yarmoliuk and issued a red card for serious foul play.

"VAR: 'Point of contact is on the shin. He's got speed and intensity. Studs are high.'

"REF: 'After review, Everton No.6 commits a challenge that endangers his opponent's safety, making contact with the studs onto the shin. Cancelling the yellow card - and a red card.'"

Referees are asked to take into account several considerations for what counts as serious foul play including the speed of the challenge, its intensity, force and what degree of control there was.

But, as always, there was plenty of debate about whether it was the correct decision.

BBC Sport's football issues correspondent Dale Johnson, said: "Really not sure about this as a VAR red card.

"Yes, Tarkowski absolutely ticks the boxes for speed and intensity and leading high with studs showing.

"But the question marks are that Tarkowski made only small contact and didn't have a straight leg when he did so.

"Maybe his reputation played a part? Remember, he wrongly escaped a VAR red card against Liverpool for a challenge, which was along the same lines. He won the ball and then followed through into Alexis Mac Allister. Thought that was a far stronger challenge."

BBC Radio 5 Live's - and former Blackburn Rovers striker - Chris Sutton, said on X: "Come on that's not a red… the game's gone."

Former Arsenal striker Alan Smith agreed the decision was harsh. He told Sky Sports: "Ten years ago we wouldn't have looked at it once and now we still [frame] it on the follow-through. I just can't see it.

"Only Tarkowski knows if he wanted to leave it high or if it was natural. The follow-through was just natural momentum.

"There's a bit of anger in there from Tarkowski and it's a little high but only he knows if he wanted to leave a little more on Yarmoliuk there."

Opinion was far from unanimous though, with both pundits in the Sky Sports studio adamant it was a clear red.

Former Liverpool centre-back Jamie Carragher said: "It's a red card. Tarkowski has got previous for tackles like that. He is a 90s defender, he tackles like that.

"He follows through with such force, it is excessive. You want to give him the benefit of the doubt but it's a red card."

He added: "You could argue was it a big enough mistake for VAR to get involved but I think we are splitting hairs. He doesn't need to do this."

While ex-Tottenham defender Toby Alderweireld added: "It's a red card, he knows what he is doing. 100%."

Josh, Sheffield: Never a red for Tarkowski and I'm a Liverpool fan. What's he meant to do? Stop momentum. It's a good tackle and the player runs into the natural follow through

Robin, Essex: Another game ruined by VAR! Not straight leg tackle you can surely see he turned his foot around. Poor!

Rob, Manchester: These sorts of VAR decisions are making me turn off football. Why pay all that money to watch arbitrary decisions impact the game?

Lee: It is a sad day when a good tackle gets a player sent off. You slow anything down and dissect it you can find wrongs. Yellow was a bit much and the red ridiculous, we need ex players in the VAR decisions too.

Max, Oldham: What a load of nonsense the red card is. Tarkowski can't stop his momentum. VAR has ruined another game, plus what is the ref doing? He had a chance to stick with the yellow card. Another case of an official who has never played the game.

Paul, St Asaph: Tarkowski has got away with that same foul a few times. Do think he's the type of player to leave one in on purpose.

Anon: Yes it's a red - Tarkowski knows what he's doing, it's frustration and wanting to leave a bit on the player.

Chris, Chelmsford: He does it all the time at the borderline but about time he got one.

Woody, London: Lack of refinement masked as passion, classic Tarkowski tackle there… glad to see him off.

George, Birmingham: Studs up in a tackle, he has to go. A clear red card for me.

Sports.text:
After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Konstantinos Tzolakis (Hull City): If you watched the Brighton game and wondered how on earth Hull won it was because Konstantinos Tzolakis was in goal. An unbelievable performance with five or six top-class saves. Big moments, big personality, he has stepped up every time. He's been one of the players of the season - I know it's a bit too early to crown people but if it stopped now he has to be goalkeeper of the season.

James Hill (Bournemouth): He backed up getting into the England squad. Sometimes when people get called up they start to get above their stations but he didn't do that at all. He was in a really good state of form. A cheeky assist as well but defensively solid. He has been in my team a few times now - a centre-half who does his job without complaining.

Malick Thiaw (Newcastle): He divides opinion but he played really well and got his goal.

Keane Lewis-Potter (Brentford): Two goals against Everton and that was before the sending-off of James Tarkowski. Performed well again. Sneaky bargain buy of the century to be honest.

Noah Okafor (Leeds): Two goals again. Leeds battered Chelsea and made them look unbelievably average. Nobody has been talking about how sneaky good Leeds have been, some really big performances this season.

Jack Rudoni (Coventry): Two assists in a must-win game against Crystal Palace. He stepped up big, fair play to him.

Elliot Anderson (Manchester City): The only person who actually showed a pulse in this game. He got a goal and showed pace and showed he wanted to be there. He tried his best to win a game of football.

Luca Williams-Barnett (Tottenham): Young man, a with goal and an assist. He just gave Spurs a spark we haven't seen for probably six or seven years now. He gave them that spark instantly and fair play to De Zerbi for putting him in. All the money spent, who knew it would be a home-grown talent in their youth team who would step up and really get the Spurs fans excited.

Florian Wirtz (Liverpool): Unbelievable performance. He has had a bit of a purple patch since Jurgen Klopp has taken over Germany. Did really well in terms of finding the gaps, drifting between players and finding through balls and now adding goals. Now we are seeing the player we saw in Germany and I am buzzing for him.

Oli McBurnie (Hull City): The man of the moment. He works really hard, he does everything for the team to make sure they are there. He is solid defensively but then he gets two shots and two goals. Top performance from him.

Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool): He made Diogo Dalot look like he'd never played a game before, not the fact he has played over 250 games for Manchester United and has gone to World Cups with Portugal and made him look childish, Ran him every time and twisted him inside out and got his goal.

Sports.title: Ellie Kildunne: Bristol star responds to Harlequins time-keeping reports
Sports.text:
England and Bristol Bears full-back Ellie Kildunne marked her return to former club Harlequins with two tries, victory and a pointed reference to reports that her poor time-keeping was behind her Stoop exit.

Kildunne, with a watch drawn on taping around her wrist, ran in two first-half tries in a 48-21 victory at the Stoop in the first round of the PWR on Sunday.

"You've all seen the headlines. Why would I have a watch on my wrist?" the 27-year-old told TNT Sport after the match.

She later posted a photo of the watch drawing on Instagram, external with the caption: "Right on time."

Kildunne, who was not quoted in Quins' announcement of her departure in June, subsequently said she was "gutted" to be leaving and that it was "as much a shock to me as everyone else".

She signed for Bristol two weeks later.

The Bears, who also signed Wales back row Bethan Lewis in the summer, finished eighth in the nine-team top flight last season.

Kildunne was not the only England star to enjoy success against the former club, with Tatyana Heard, who was part of big-spending Sale's summer recruitment drive, enjoying a 31-17 win over Gloucester-Hartpury.

Gloucester-Hartpury, who won the title three times in a row between 2023 and 2025, are without a head coach after Dan Murphy left on the eve of the season.

Champions Saracens and Ealing Trailfinders, who lost to Saracens in June's final, best Leicester and Loughborough Lightning respectively.

Sports.title: Freddie Potts loving life in Belgium with Club Brugge
Sports.text:
When Liverpool visit Club Brugge on Wednesday they are likely to come up against English midfielder Freddie Potts.

The 23-year-old ended a 16-year association with West Ham in the summer to join the Belgian champions for an undisclosed fee.

And he has started every game, bar one missed through suspension, in all competitions.

After losing to Aston Villa in the Champions League, they have defeated Inter Milan, Lens and PSV.

"It really is a dream because you hear the music and then you see your family in the stands and you remember all the times that you watched Champions League on TV," Potts told BBC Radio 5 Live's Euro Leagues Show.

"You think of all the memories that you make watching it and to be playing in it now is something that every kid dreams of."

Potts' whole life had been based around West Ham. He had been with the club since the age of six and his father Steve, who made 506 appearances for the Hammers, is a first-team coach.

Potts Jr played 28 times for West Ham, with 25 of them coming last season as they were relegated from the Premier League.

He also had loan spells with Wycombe in League One and Portsmouth in the Championship.

"In pre-season my minutes with West Ham were limited, they weren't as much as I wanted and then I spoke with my agent and said 'let's explore options because this season I'm 22, turning 23'," Potts said.

"It's a massive part of my career and I wanted to play. The opportunity of Club Brugge came along with Champions League football, the best club in Belgium and it was an opportunity I couldn't really turn down with how my minutes were going down with West Ham.

"I grew up in the area, going to the stadium watching the games. It was always going to be a tough decision but it was something that I had to do for my career.

"It was an emotional decision because it had to be made quite quickly. It's been the right decision for me and so far I'm enjoying it, I'm loving life here."

Club Brugge won the Belgian title last season and are second, just one point behind leaders Union Saint-Gilloise this campaign.

"It's a physical league," said Potts. "My running and physical stats have been higher than they've ever been. It's a demanding league in that way.

"Club Brugge demands a lot, from winning the ball back and going man for man in the press. And your responsibility off the ball is something that you have to take really seriously."

Sports.title: Marco Penge: Englishman secures PGA Tour card for 2027 with win
Sports.text:
The RSM Classic - round four leaderboard

M Penge (Eng) wins play-off

-16 L Haotong (Chn), M Greyserman (US), M Penge (Eng), M Thorbjornsen (US); -14 R Hojgaard (Den), J Koivun (US)

Selected others: -13 H English (US); -11 B Koepka (US); -9 H Hall (Eng); -8 M Pavon (Fra); -5 J Smith (Eng)

England's Marco Penge birdied the first extra hole in a four-man play-off to win the RSM Classic in Georgia and secure his PGA Tour card for 2027.

Penge's five-under 65 in a delayed final round at the Sea Island Resort's Seaside Course had left him tied at 16 under overall, with American duo Max Greyserman and Michael Thorbjornsen, and China's Li Haotong.

However, Penge produced a superb iron shot and drained a birdie putt from no more than five feet to claim his first triumph on the main professional tour in North America and the $1.3m (£993,000) top prize.

"I proved to myself I can do it under the most immense pressure. I always seem to play my best golf when my back is up against the wall," Penge said.

"I've been through this before on the DP World Tour, keeping my card in the last event and dealing with adversity and coming back from health issues, all that stuff, so I knew I could do it.

"I just wasn't sure I had the game this week to be able to do it. Thankfully I did."

Penge started the week 120th in the FedExCup standings and required at least a top-four finish to jump inside the top 100 places and guarantee his full playing status on the PGA Tour next term.

And having picked up four strokes on the back nine, which included a birdie on the 18th to reach the play-off, he achieved his objective in style.

"Of course we're trying to win golf tournaments but the first task for me was to keep my card," Penge said.

"When I got on that 18th tee in the play-off, I was like, 'OK, I can win the golf tournament now'."

Penge, who has previously won three times on the DP World Tour, has endured a stop-start campaign, having taken a six-week break following the US PGA Championship to deal with a viral illness and vertigo.

"It's a lot of hard work to get back to feeling myself," Penge added.

"When I came back, I felt like I was actually in a good spot and playing some good golf. I've been putting the work in and I said to my team as long as I give everything I can then the result is the result and if I lose my card then it is what it is."

With heavy rain forcing Saturday's third round to be postponed until Sunday, it meant the final round on Monday was played without fans being present as the event did not have enough volunteers to manage spectators.

Sports.title: MotoGP: Is Marc Marquez, Valentino Rossi or Giacomo Agostini the sport's greatest of all time?
Sports.text:
As Marc Marquez ascended a staircase, the silhouette of a goat matched his every step.

It was a nod to his increasing - or solidified, depending on who you ask - status as MotoGP's 'greatest of all time' (GOAT).

In winning the 2026 championship in Portugal on Sunday, Spain's Marquez secured his eighth overall title, the first per son in the modern era to achieve this accolade.

It drew the Ducati rider level with the great Giacomo Agostini, who won his eight titles between 1966-75.

And yet it is Valentino Rossi, who Marquez has now surpassed for World Championship crowns, who most view as his biggest rival for GOAT status.

"I feel proud when the fans and media say that I am one of the greatest of all time," Marquez told BBC Sport on Monday.

"I do not agree when they say I am the greatest because every athlete in motorsport has their moments, their career and injuries and I respect all of them, all the legends."

But despite his humility, is 33-year-old Marquez actually the sport's greatest? Have your say at the bottom of this article.

In winning his eighth premier class championship on Sunday, Marquez overcame the biggest points deficit in MotoGP history - 102 points - to take the title.

But Marquez is the ultimate comeback king.

Last year, he won his first title in six years, a period in which he overcame 109 crashes, multiple injuries including a broken arm, ankle, ribs and fingers, and a severe concussion.

In 2023 he told BBC Sport he was "not ready to win again" and at the end of that season finished 14th in the standings. He then left Honda, a team where he won six titles, to join Gresini Racing, the satellite Ducati team.

After a solid 2024 season, in which he claimed three feature race wins and two pole positions, he joined the factory Ducati team and now has two titles in two seasons with the Italian outfit.

But 2026 was not without its issues. Marquez was without a win when he arrived at the French Grand Prix in May, and things went from bad to worse after he suffered a crash in the sprint race at Le Mans and had to have operations on his foot and shoulder. He then missed the next round in Barcelona.

Marquez made his return at Mugello 20 days later, facing that hefty points deficit, to the then leader Marco Bezzecchi.

"In that moment after the crash in Le Mans and then the seventh surgery on the right shoulder, [my title charge] was completely over. I was in hospital. I was 102 points behind the leader and I was not the fastest rider on the track," said Marquez.

"Then I say OK you can believe in me, but if you are not the fastest you cannot recover points. Then I tried to be very focused, to work on the mental side and to understand where my level was. I accepted that the level was key during the season and I had to take points and wait for my moment."

Marquez then won seven of the next 13 grand prix races, twice missing out on the chance to seal the title in Qatar and Saturday's sprint race in the Algarve, before finally clinching the win with one race weekend to come in Valencia.

While Sunday marked his eighth MotoGP title, it was Marquez's 10th championship overall after wins in the 125cc and Moto2 categories on his journey to the top of the sport.

Let's look at the case for Rossi.

The Italian is a motorcycle racing legend and still has a cult like status around the world, even after retiring in 2021.

Rossi is a seven-time MotoGP champion, with nine world titles to his name.

The now 47-year-old remains the only rider in history to win World Championships in 125cc, 250cc, 500cc and MotoGP.

Rossi has a record 89 victories in the premier class but Marquez is closing the gap with 80.

Marquez is still the only rider to win a MotoGP championship in his rookie year and after that dominated the series, with six titles in seven seasons between 2013 and 2019.

He and Rossi do share some MotoGP history. They are the only two riders to have won at least two world titles with two different manufacturers.

The rivalry between Rossi and Marquez is legendary.

In 2013 their battle at the Corkscrew at Laguna Seca became infamous, with Marquez eventually taking the win.

The crashes have been dramatic too. In 2015 in Sepang, the pair collided with Marquez crashing out, resulting in a back-of-the-grid penalty for Rossi which ultimately cost him that year's title.

Rossi has continually claimed that his younger challenger deliberately sabotaged his championship hopes, admitting in a recent interview on Italian TV that "it still stings".

Two years later, in Argentina, the riders came to blows again, this time with Rossi hitting the tarmac.

At one time Rossi accused Marquez of "destroying" the sport, with Marquez stating their relationship was like a "divorce".

"It is a big pleasure to equal Giacomo Agostini in premier class titles," said Marquez.

"He is the greatest of all time."

But in the modern era, does Marquez have the edge?

With a contract at Ducati extended until 2028 you would not rule him out of winning more titles in the future, but for now, Marquez is revelling in the present.

"I want to enjoy the moment, this week," he said.

"I want to enjoy the next weekend in Valencia. That is a special weekend because it is in a Spanish city and [I will] celebrate the world championship there, and then we will have time to prepare for 2027."
