GeneralTab.title: Analysis: Can Andy Burnham turn volume down on UK rejoining EU debate?
GeneralTab.text:
When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.

It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader, promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe.

And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave.

Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again.

All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election.

Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said.

But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."

So he might offer a referendum. Or he might not.

He also suggested the frequency of his public utterances on the subject may be limited, insisting there would be no "running commentary," offering instead what he called "a calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interest in the long term."

Plus, he said Europe could change in the coming years. A nod, without naming her, that Marine Le Pen could become president of France, for instance. How might that shift the debate?

Burnham's willingness to repeatedly talk about the European question in the last few months has, inevitably, spawned quite the reaction.

A campaign group, Stay Out, has got itself up and running to argue exactly that.

And the European Movement is helping launch a rival outfit called, again, you guessed it, Get In.

It is a reminder that that the EU question has a knack of getting under the skin of British politics, often to the exclusion of other things, sometimes to the exclusion of seemingly everything.

Can the prime minister successfully manage the volume switch so the topic is background hubbub in 2027, rather than a deafening din?

Meanwhile, what does the European Union itself make of all of this? EU sources see Andy Burnham's desire to "brainstorm" with them what the future relationship might look like as "normal diplomacy" as one figure put it, adding: "I don't think there are many options. And they are clear. The status quo. The customs union. The single market. And full membership."

They mirror his expectation that "brainstorming" won't involve additional meetings, let alone a structured set of bespoke talks arriving at a conclusion. "We don't need a template. It will be part of the regular discussion," is how it was put to me.

On Thursday, the government will publish its European Partnerships Bill, the legislation needed to enact, at the UK end, the agreements reached at the summit. Also later this week, the legal text of those agreements is due to be published – the small print of which will be pored over.

How much might the UK have to compensate the EU for, for instance, if a future government were to decide to reverse the changes that have just been signed up to? Within the deal it is expected that were Britain to change its mind on the food export part of the deal in the next 10 years, Brussels would charge London for the reinstallation of the checkpoints that will soon no longer be needed.

Then, there are the ongoing negotiations between the two sides about unresolved areas of potential cooperation. The EU has made much of its desire to secure a deal on university tuition fees in the next six months, with the hope that EU students will pay no more at UK universities than British students do. The deal would be reciprocal for UK students studying elsewhere in Europe. Both sides think an agreement is within reach. Senior figures in Whitehall are also encouraged by the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan to protect European industry from China. Then there is the EU's common electricity market.

But even if all these things are agreed – and they will all provoke debate here about whether or not they are good ideas – Andy Burnham has publicly said incremental changes only take the UK so far.

It is clear he has an appetite and an interest in going further. The question, ultimately, is how much further?

GeneralTab.title: Timms report to suggest faster Pip payments for some disabled people
GeneralTab.text:
A review into the main disability benefit is set to recommend that those with the most severe conditions and terminal illnesses should get quicker payments.

The report on Personal Independence Payment (Pip) will also suggest overhauling assessments so they provide claimants in England and Wales with more appropriate support.

But it is understood not to suggest major savings, despite the benefit's cost being projected to more than double between 2020 and 2030.

Groups representing disabled people - who had a hand in drafting the report - have broadly welcomed its findings.

About four million people claim Pip, which is set to cost about £32bn this financial year, a figure projected to rise to £41.5bn in 2030-31. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

Chaired by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms, the review was set up last year after the Starmer government's aborted attempt to cut welfare spending.

Sir Stephen has proposed linking disability benefit payments to real-life needs and that extra costs be incurred by the claimant.

Those with the most severe and persistent conditions would be fast-tracked with no further assessments involved - believed to be the case for about one in 10 claimants - with the aim of creating a "less burdensome" process, Sir Stephen wrote in The Times.

There were concerns from disability charities that Pip payments might become means-tested or the cash payments partially replaced with vouchers, but it is understood this will not be the case.

Frankie Bowyer from Scope UK told the BBC that disabled people found the assessment process "stressful and degrading".

"People have described to us feeling that assessors were trying to catch them out, trying to minimise their needs and that's really not want we want to see," Bowyer said.

Alicia Cartwright in Preston receives the higher rate of Pip for both the daily living and mobility components, which she says equates to about £500 every four weeks.

The mum-of-two, a trained benefits adviser, told the BBC that even she found the current assessment process "intimidating and confusing".

"Trust disabled people to know what their needs are. Of course, have some checks in there, absolutely, but we really need to start from a place of trust.

"Currently, in any dealings with the benefits system, you feel like you're on trial, and for a lot of people, asking for help is difficult in the first place."

Cartwright is a power wheelchair user and works several part-time jobs at a university. She says the costs of her disabilities run to a further £1,500 a month which she has to pay out of her wages.

"The mobility part of it, that goes on paying for my wheelchair. And then the rest of my Pip goes entirely on paying someone to help me around the house," she said.

Matt Ryder from the Adam Smith Institute, a free-market think tank said disability claims had risen fastest amongst young people "who are the least likely to be become seriously ill as a result of the pandemic".

"We need to target lower-level mental health claims. That seems to be the root cause of the rising claims, so we need to restrict eligibility for that," he said.

"It's where the cost is heading... According to the OBR, we can expect that spending on Pip will rise to £47bn in five years' time. And there's no reason why it would stop at that point. Why wouldn't it continue on growing?"

Research last month from the Resolution Foundation, a think tank focused on lower and middle earners, suggested about one in six Pip recipients said they didn't incur any extra costs due to their disability.

It suggested removing Pip from this group would save up to £4.4m a year.

Lindsay Judge from the Resolution Foundation said although the Timms Review did not set out to cut costs, this "should be possible nonetheless" and that "major change is needed".

She said improvements should include assessments that "better understand disabled people's needs" as well as awards in the form of cash or services that "better reflect the actual costs that disabled people face" as well as "more regular light touch check-ins so that changes of circumstances are fully understood".

The review's proposals will be put forward by a steering group, led by Sir Stephen, which the government will respond to.

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales, but the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

GeneralTab.title: BBC exposes Whitby dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each
GeneralTab.text:
When Katie Thornton paid £2,000 for a nine-week-old puppy for her son, she knew it was a premium price - but was happy to be doing business with a "legit", council-approved breeder.

But Ozzy the Dobermann pup started coughing in the car on the way home, and within 48 hours he was in a veterinary hospital receiving urgent treatment for pneumonia.

Since then, his ongoing health problems mean Katie has racked up more than £5,000 in vet bills.

A BBC investigation has found the breeder had been stripped of his five-star rating two months before selling several sick puppies, but continued to advertise as five-star.

We have also found at least 15 other breeders in England advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than it really is.

An expert reviewing our findings - including undercover footage we recorded at the breeder's home - said the investigation exposes a nationwide "wild west" of dog licensing, making it "easy for consumers to be scammed".

The breeder has not responded to our request for comment.

When Katie visited the premises of Mikjulora Dobermanns in Whitby, North Yorkshire, she said the puppies' mother "didn't look very well" and was "skinny" and "shaking".

But she felt the breeder, Michael Estill, was "pushing me to buy Ozzy" so she paid for him and took him home on the spot.

Katie defended her decision because she had done extensive research to check the business was "legit".

The mother-of-one, from Harrogate, said she had checked his licence number and read through his website and online adverts, which said he had decades of experience and a "five-star" breeding licence.

In England, local councils grant breeders in their area a licence and star rating dependent on welfare standards.

Vet reports for North Yorkshire Council from August and December 2025, seen by the BBC, cited dozens of concerns with Estill's business, including:

"Poor" living conditions "akin to a prison", with dogs kept in cages, stacked on top of each other, that were too small for them to turn around in

Deteriorating health and welfare of "sad" dogs

Puppies for sale not matching descriptions - "in other words it is a scam"

Prospective buyers "very vulnerable to unsuspectingly purchasing unhealthy puppies"

The business was "more or less a puppy farm masquerading as an honest and conscientious breeder. This must stop"

Estill "bullied" a local vet to perform an "unnecessary" Caesarean section on one of his dogs, to reduce the time he would have to spend monitoring her

His "demanding" behaviour led the practice to give him several doses of a powerful stimulant which he gave to one of his dogs at home - which the vet considered to be "negligent"

He had a three-year-old dog euthanised because he suspected her to have a neurological condition, despite the vet encouraging him to get diagnostic tests and specialist treatment first.

Following the reports, which concluded that the business was "functioning outside the law", the council renewed Estill's licence in January but downgraded his rating from five-star (the highest standards) to one-star (minor failings).

GeneralTab.title: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
GeneralTab.text:
There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.

Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.

The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.

All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.

This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.

The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.

And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board.

This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September, where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.

Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument.

There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.

Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.

This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.

The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.

Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres.

A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach.

The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment.

The Democrats in Congress have vowed to investigate both the President and Mr Huang, and he is due to appear before them next week. Jensen Huang is at the centre of it all - the technology, the financing, the US politics and the geopolitics.

Today has proven Jensen Huang was in fact, too big to fire.

GeneralTab.title: I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it
GeneralTab.text:
Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.

Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it.

"I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.

Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.

Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load".

The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.

Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present.

"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.

The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic.

The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.

Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.

Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

Some of the larger tasks her team has faced over the years include flying from Austin to New York City to buy a desperately needed Christmas gift, and finding a new wedding location for a client with just three days' notice due to an incoming hurricane.

Many more women than men use these companies.

Queen of To Do says just 20% of its clients are male, while only one of Life Laundry's 25 clients is a man.

Some of that disparity is likely due to mothers still looking after the lion's share of household admin, as studies continue to show.

However, Life Laundry's Forbes wonders if some men are too proud to ask for assistance.

"Men are struggling as well, but I think they're less likely to ask for help."

articles.title: Analysis: Can Andy Burnham turn volume down on UK rejoining EU debate?
articles.text:
When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.

It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader, promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe.

And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave.

Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again.

All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election.

Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said.

But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."

So he might offer a referendum. Or he might not.

He also suggested the frequency of his public utterances on the subject may be limited, insisting there would be no "running commentary," offering instead what he called "a calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interest in the long term."

Plus, he said Europe could change in the coming years. A nod, without naming her, that Marine Le Pen could become president of France, for instance. How might that shift the debate?

Burnham's willingness to repeatedly talk about the European question in the last few months has, inevitably, spawned quite the reaction.

A campaign group, Stay Out, has got itself up and running to argue exactly that.

And the European Movement is helping launch a rival outfit called, again, you guessed it, Get In.

It is a reminder that that the EU question has a knack of getting under the skin of British politics, often to the exclusion of other things, sometimes to the exclusion of seemingly everything.

Can the prime minister successfully manage the volume switch so the topic is background hubbub in 2027, rather than a deafening din?

Meanwhile, what does the European Union itself make of all of this? EU sources see Andy Burnham's desire to "brainstorm" with them what the future relationship might look like as "normal diplomacy" as one figure put it, adding: "I don't think there are many options. And they are clear. The status quo. The customs union. The single market. And full membership."

They mirror his expectation that "brainstorming" won't involve additional meetings, let alone a structured set of bespoke talks arriving at a conclusion. "We don't need a template. It will be part of the regular discussion," is how it was put to me.

On Thursday, the government will publish its European Partnerships Bill, the legislation needed to enact, at the UK end, the agreements reached at the summit. Also later this week, the legal text of those agreements is due to be published – the small print of which will be pored over.

How much might the UK have to compensate the EU for, for instance, if a future government were to decide to reverse the changes that have just been signed up to? Within the deal it is expected that were Britain to change its mind on the food export part of the deal in the next 10 years, Brussels would charge London for the reinstallation of the checkpoints that will soon no longer be needed.

Then, there are the ongoing negotiations between the two sides about unresolved areas of potential cooperation. The EU has made much of its desire to secure a deal on university tuition fees in the next six months, with the hope that EU students will pay no more at UK universities than British students do. The deal would be reciprocal for UK students studying elsewhere in Europe. Both sides think an agreement is within reach. Senior figures in Whitehall are also encouraged by the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan to protect European industry from China. Then there is the EU's common electricity market.

But even if all these things are agreed – and they will all provoke debate here about whether or not they are good ideas – Andy Burnham has publicly said incremental changes only take the UK so far.

It is clear he has an appetite and an interest in going further. The question, ultimately, is how much further?

articles.title: Timms report to suggest faster Pip payments for some disabled people
articles.text:
A review into the main disability benefit is set to recommend that those with the most severe conditions and terminal illnesses should get quicker payments.

The report on Personal Independence Payment (Pip) will also suggest overhauling assessments so they provide claimants in England and Wales with more appropriate support.

But it is understood not to suggest major savings, despite the benefit's cost being projected to more than double between 2020 and 2030.

Groups representing disabled people - who had a hand in drafting the report - have broadly welcomed its findings.

About four million people claim Pip, which is set to cost about £32bn this financial year, a figure projected to rise to £41.5bn in 2030-31. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

Chaired by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms, the review was set up last year after the Starmer government's aborted attempt to cut welfare spending.

Sir Stephen has proposed linking disability benefit payments to real-life needs and that extra costs be incurred by the claimant.

Those with the most severe and persistent conditions would be fast-tracked with no further assessments involved - believed to be the case for about one in 10 claimants - with the aim of creating a "less burdensome" process, Sir Stephen wrote in The Times.

There were concerns from disability charities that Pip payments might become means-tested or the cash payments partially replaced with vouchers, but it is understood this will not be the case.

Frankie Bowyer from Scope UK told the BBC that disabled people found the assessment process "stressful and degrading".

"People have described to us feeling that assessors were trying to catch them out, trying to minimise their needs and that's really not want we want to see," Bowyer said.

Alicia Cartwright in Preston receives the higher rate of Pip for both the daily living and mobility components, which she says equates to about £500 every four weeks.

The mum-of-two, a trained benefits adviser, told the BBC that even she found the current assessment process "intimidating and confusing".

"Trust disabled people to know what their needs are. Of course, have some checks in there, absolutely, but we really need to start from a place of trust.

"Currently, in any dealings with the benefits system, you feel like you're on trial, and for a lot of people, asking for help is difficult in the first place."

Cartwright is a power wheelchair user and works several part-time jobs at a university. She says the costs of her disabilities run to a further £1,500 a month which she has to pay out of her wages.

"The mobility part of it, that goes on paying for my wheelchair. And then the rest of my Pip goes entirely on paying someone to help me around the house," she said.

Matt Ryder from the Adam Smith Institute, a free-market think tank said disability claims had risen fastest amongst young people "who are the least likely to be become seriously ill as a result of the pandemic".

"We need to target lower-level mental health claims. That seems to be the root cause of the rising claims, so we need to restrict eligibility for that," he said.

"It's where the cost is heading... According to the OBR, we can expect that spending on Pip will rise to £47bn in five years' time. And there's no reason why it would stop at that point. Why wouldn't it continue on growing?"

Research last month from the Resolution Foundation, a think tank focused on lower and middle earners, suggested about one in six Pip recipients said they didn't incur any extra costs due to their disability.

It suggested removing Pip from this group would save up to £4.4m a year.

Lindsay Judge from the Resolution Foundation said although the Timms Review did not set out to cut costs, this "should be possible nonetheless" and that "major change is needed".

She said improvements should include assessments that "better understand disabled people's needs" as well as awards in the form of cash or services that "better reflect the actual costs that disabled people face" as well as "more regular light touch check-ins so that changes of circumstances are fully understood".

The review's proposals will be put forward by a steering group, led by Sir Stephen, which the government will respond to.

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales, but the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

articles.title: BBC exposes Whitby dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each
articles.text:

Puppies for sale not matching descriptions - "in other words it is a scam"

Prospective buyers "very vulnerable to unsuspectingly purchasing unhealthy puppies"

articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.text:
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.

"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.

A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.

"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

articles.title: State failing to keep public safe, warns victims' commissioner
articles.text:
The victims' commissioner for England and Wales has said the state is failing to keep the public safe, as she urged Andy Burnham to put the justice system at the heart of his 10-year plan for government.

Claire Waxman told the BBC that she would press the prime minister to commit to reforms in the decade-long blueprint, which he is set to unveil next month.

She warned that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding in jails, along with long waits in the courts, had eroded the trust of crime victims to come forward.

It comes as the commissioner's latest annual survey of victims, to be published on Tuesday, found many had experienced long waits for justice.

Nearly half of respondents whose case went to a crown court had seen their trial postponed, with over a quarter reporting the trial had taken place more than a year after it was originally scheduled.

Almost half of the respondents to the survey also said they were dissatisfied with communication from the police.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Waxman said the results showed victims were being failed "at every point".

The commissioner, who said she was due to meet Burnham in the coming weeks, said she wanted him to put a "real commitment to reforming our criminal justice system" as part of his 10-year plan.

"It's been under-invested and mismanaged for so many years. That's why we're in the state that we're in," she added.

She warned: "It can't continue. Otherwise I will be in a position as the victims' commissioner to have to be very honest and open with victims publicly to say there's no point coming forward and reporting."

Asked whether the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe, she replied: "It is failing", adding that the early release of prisoners could lead to the potentially risky offenders being supervised by a probation service "on its knees".

Waxman also criticised the government's handling of the scheme, saying that victims needed further reassurance that they would be kept safe when offenders are let out under the programme to ease overcrowding in jails.

Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to eventually be released under the latest version of the scheme, the need for which Labour has blamed on a lack of investment in prisons under the Conservatives.

Waxman said that letters sent over the summer to warn victims ahead of releases had been "very poor" and lacked detail on how offenders were going to be risk-assessed prior to being let out early.

She said she was "still waiting to see" data about the impact of releases on the ground, adding it had been around a year since the last meeting of the National Criminal Justice Board, an oversight body for the justice system.

articles.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
articles.text:
Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.

The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.

The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."

"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.

The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.

French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.

In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.

"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.

Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.

French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".

"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.

Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".

Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.

Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.

Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

articles.title: Why I don't always tell potential employers I'm dyslexic
articles.text:
Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her.

"It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.

A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.

Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.

Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.

But the world of work has proved more challenging.

For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.

In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."

One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.

Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities.

"I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."

She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.

articles.title: First Children's Booker prize reveals shortlist ' full of surprises' - and its child judges
articles.text:
The first ever Children's Booker Prize has announced the eight books in the running for the new £50,000 award.

Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories are on the shortlist, which is aimed at children aged eight to 12.

The authors in contention include former Children's Laureate of Ireland Eoin Colfer, who is best known for his Artemis Fowl series, and teacher and children's author Catherine Bruton.

Four children have also been announced as new judges after a UK-wide competition. Twelve-year-old Ibrahim from Hampshire was one of those picked from more than 4,000 entrants.

He told me he was called back into school for a phone call with chair of judges Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who broke the news. Ibrahim said he couldn't be happier.

"First Children's Booker Prize judge! On my CV - that's going to take me a long way… I'm too overwhelmed to even be excited."

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC "it's really, really important that this is a prize for children's books. Having judges who are children will be proof of that… If the children don't love a book, it won't win."

Ibrahim, his fellow child judges and Cottrell-Boyce will be joined on the judging panel by Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, who owns an award-winning children's book shop in north London.

Ibrahim said he loves reading "because it's just a way to unwind yourself from the outside world. If you get stuck in a book, you're not getting your face out of there until you finish it".

He's far too professional to share which books on the list he likes best, but he told me when he was reading one of them recently: "I had to tell my mum to confiscate it because I couldn't stop reading it and I was getting a headache."

Cottrell-Boyce said he isn't concerned over whether the adult judges might dominate the decision-making.

"If - like me - you've been visiting schools as a children's writer for 20 years, it's a rare thing to meet a child who is too over-awed to express an opinion. They're usually very forthright".

Ibrahim proves that point. He told me "the adults are not going to control that meeting… 100% not!"

He's looking for "something that has different perspectives, you can see it in a different way. New characters, not just the same old sloppy characters that authors make all the time. They just make these books that just have the same plot line".

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC the range of subjects was "amazing".

"Children's books can be about anything, can deal with anything. But the tone has to convey hope. I can't think of a darker childhood than the one endured by Anne of Green Gables. I also can't think of a more joyous book than Anne of Green Gables."

He acknowledges the worrying statistics on reading. The National Literacy Trust's Annual Literacy Survey last year showed the percentage of children and young people who said they enjoyed reading was its lowest in 20 years. Just one in three aged eight to 18 said they enjoyed reading in their free time, down by more than a third since 2005.

"That's why we're here! To fight the fight. To make sure our children have as many opportunities as possible to discover how pleasurable, how bonding, how thrilling and enriching and fortifying it can be to slip out of the prison of the present into the infinity of the story."

Ibrahim told me "my friends don't read books at all".

He doesn't try to persuade them. "I let them live their life. I live my life".

But if he were to try to, what would he say?

"Put a timer on your phone, make sure it's blocked and then they'll decide to do something more productive. I might be able to convince them... because it can help you with English, your confidence, and help you build self esteem."

For him, though, the best thing about a book is when it takes him into another world. "If you try to take your head out of it, it makes you think 'oh my god what's going to happen next?'"

The winning book will be announced in February next year at the Young V&A in London. 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books will be given to children who need them most.

articles.title: Britain's landlords are getting bigger. A two-tier rental market may follow
articles.text:
On Christmas Eve 2021, there was a knock on the door of Lexi Levens' rented flat. It was a letter sent by special delivery from the NHS nurse's landlord saying she, her husband, and four children had two months to move out.

"The kids all thought it was a present arriving," she recalls.

Lexi's landlord had used something known then as a Section 21 notice to evict her family without needing to give a reason.

Lexi, along with the housing charity Shelter, went on to lobby the government to improve rights for renters. The Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May this year, banned Section 21 evictions and also made it illegal to refuse to rent to people based on their status as a family with children.

The landlords Lexi had been renting from at that time were typical of the English housing market — individuals who owned one or a handful of properties.

Many of these small landlords say the Renters' Rights Act has left them feeling squeezed. They also say rising interest rates, new regulations and tax changes (including some in the most recent Budget) are making things harder. Some say they are selling up.

Meanwhile, according to Savills estate agents, 2026 is likely to be another record year for investment from large institutions in what is known in the property industry as build to rent (BTR). This is when big developers build blocks of flats or family housing to rent out, something that is commonplace in parts of Europe and the US. It means that rather than dealing with an individual landlord or letting agent, tenants are instead renting from larger, typically corporate, entities.

So does the shift, as some believe, represent a welcome professionalisation of the UK rental sector? Or will renters increasingly miss the positive elements of the personal touch that small landlords can provide?

According to the latest government survey of private landlords in England, 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, representing 51% of tenancies.

And according to 2024 research by real estate agency Savills, around 40% rental homes in the US and Germany are owned by large institutions — be they private firms, listed companies, pension funds, or co-operatives. For the UK, Savills calculated that figure was just 3%.

But the rental market is changing. The trend is most visible in England, where BTR has boomed in large cities and where regulations like the Renters' Rights Act apply, but there are BTR developments in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland too and the devolved nations are also seeing increased regulation on landlords, such as with Scotland's rent controls.

Lexi is pleased with the idea of a sector with stricter rules for landlords and more professional institutions getting involved.

"Anything that takes away from landlords having personal preferences [around choosing who they are or not prepared to rent to]… is a good thing," she says, adding that she believes large, corporate landlords would be less likely to act that way.

Not everyone is convinced BTR landlords are better, though.

Clint Stevenson, a 44-year-old magician for weddings and events, has been renting his one-bedroom flat in Ramsgate for £550 a month for two years. He says he has "the most amazing landlady" — an older woman who he regularly chats to. He sometimes walks her dog and does her shopping as well.

He says he had considered renting from a BTR development, but found the accommodation to be "very industrial and very unpersonal". He also found what was on offer to be expensive compared to what he is used to paying.

"They just look like big, money-grabbing deals," he says.

In Cardiff, Grainger, the UK's largest listed BTR developer, is currently offering a fully-furnished studio flat on the 20th floor of The Copper Works in the city centre with views over the bay for £1,265 a month.

It's a lot more than what is currently on offer on Rightmove, a 15 minute walk away from the city centre – a fully-furnished, ground-floor, one-bedroom flat with a garden for £800 a month.

But tenants in The Copper Works have free access to a gym, a cinema room, a roof terrace, and a games room. There's also free WiFi, a concierge service with a helpline, and other amenities. In addition, the studio flat has an EPC B rating as opposed to an EPC C rating for the one-bedroom flat down the road.

"You have to look at what you're getting for your rent," says Helen Gordon, Grainger's chief executive. She says BTR landlords can offer these services because of their scale. As she puts it: "If you run 11,000 homes, you can afford to invest in systems, processes, people, helplines – that sort of thing – that smaller landlords can't."

Gordon strongly pushes back against suggestions that there is a lack of human connection within BTR, noting that tenants are able to speak with staff whenever they need and that the firm regularly organises events for socialising with other tenants to create a sense of community.

It's a pattern across the BTR sector: a higher price point in exchange for what is marketed as high-quality accommodation and a suite of services — some in the sector even refer to 'customers' rather than 'tenants'.

The number of BTR homes has tripled between 2019 and 2025, and while it represents just 3% of the overall rental market at the moment, Gordon believes it could reach "at least 10%" over the next ten years. "And I think it could go higher," she adds.

"If you've got major institutions that include pension funds, financial institutions, and FTSE 250 companies running the stock, it's easier to hold people to account than lots of disparate people, so you can see why it's attractive [to government]."

A 2012 government-commissioned report concluded that more BTR properties could help increase housing supply and drive economic growth as well as providing tenants with more choice and better quality housing. It recommended central government and councils support the development of BTR through favourable planning decisions and releasing public land.

There is a lot of evidence governments and local authorities listened. Local leaders in big cities – London and Manchester, in particular – have partnered with developers to deliver large housing projects involving, in many cases, the release of public land. Kings Cross in London is a prime example of this and current London Mayor Sadiq Khan's push for BTR development near Transport for London (TFL) land, mostly Tube stations, is another example. As part of that, TfL formed a joint venture with Grainger.

Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills, says it's not a matter of looking at one policy, government, or council in particular but more the "policy environment" which has been around since the 2010s.

He points to a series of tax changes, including mortgage interest tax relief changes and higher stamp duty rates for second homes and buy-to-let properties introduced by the Conservatives around 10 years ago, which made the sector less favourable for smaller landlords.

The Renters' Rights Act and more stringent energy efficiency requirements were later introduced. And the last two Budgets have raised taxes on rental income from next year. The tax change applies to individuals who are landlords, not to BTR companies which pay corporation tax, further encouraging professionalisation of the sector.

Yet, while many welcome these changes, others say they are pushing smaller landlords out of the sector. As Cook puts it, there has been more "stick" for small landlords than "carrot" for the BTR sector.

Between 2000 and 2016, a net 2.74 million homes were added to the English rental market in total, according to an analysis of government data by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. In the 10 years since, a net of just 200,000 have. For renters, it is now less likely that your property is owned by a smaller landlord.

Kevin Barber started off with one rental home. He has since grown this portfolio to 40 properties with his business partner but resents what he sees as the clout of the BTR sector. "The big property companies have got so much financial power and influence with the government," he says.

But whether we will actually see more homes being built is another matter. Savills' Cook says BTR development could slow in future as high interest rates and increased building costs continue to hit developers' bottom line. These same factors are why housebuilders say they are building less.

Cook says the current rate of BTR development won't be enough to meet the demand for rental properties on its own, at least not imminently. In addition, while some BTR developers do build cheaper family homes for rent in the suburbs, the sector is largely still building blocks of flats for wealthier renters living in cities.

This raises the possibility that the UK could end up with a two-tier rental market – what Cook describes as the "haves and the have nots" – where high-earning city-dwelling renters have their pick of rental properties but poorer renters in suburbs struggle to find somewhere to live.

Unless the government steps in, possibly by delivering more housing itself or partnering with developers to do so, it might find any positives gained by the Renters' Rights Act are undone by an increasingly fragmented rental market.

articles.title: What China's Xi Jinping could take away from Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.

Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.

But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.

That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.

Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".

Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.

Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.

For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.

Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.

The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.

Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.

But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.

Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.

Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.

The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.

The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.

China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.

And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.

He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.

If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.

What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.

Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.

What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.

Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.

Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

articles.title: Saurav Das: Cockroach Janta Party leader says he was stopped from flying to UK for Oxford event
articles.text:
A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.

Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".

It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests, said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.

He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.

"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.

A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.

Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.

"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.

Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.

In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.

The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.

There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.

In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
articles.text:
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.

On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.

This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.

articles.title: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
articles.text:
There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.

Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.

The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.

All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.

This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.

The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.

And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board.

This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September, where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.

Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument.

There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.

Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.

This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.

The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.

Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres.

A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach.

The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment.

The Democrats in Congress have vowed to investigate both the President and Mr Huang, and he is due to appear before them next week. Jensen Huang is at the centre of it all - the technology, the financing, the US politics and the geopolitics.

Today has proven Jensen Huang was in fact, too big to fire.

articles.title: I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it
articles.text:
Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.

Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it.

"I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.

Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.

Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load".

The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.

Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present.

"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.

The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic.

The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.

Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.

Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

Some of the larger tasks her team has faced over the years include flying from Austin to New York City to buy a desperately needed Christmas gift, and finding a new wedding location for a client with just three days' notice due to an incoming hurricane.

Many more women than men use these companies.

Queen of To Do says just 20% of its clients are male, while only one of Life Laundry's 25 clients is a man.

Some of that disparity is likely due to mothers still looking after the lion's share of household admin, as studies continue to show.

However, Life Laundry's Forbes wonders if some men are too proud to ask for assistance.

"Men are struggling as well, but I think they're less likely to ask for help."

articles.title: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
articles.text:
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.

Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.

Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday, with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.

Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.

Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.

While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.

A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.

Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".

"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.

"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.

"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.

"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Politicians are also demanding greater scrutiny.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."

She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

articles.title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
articles.text:
Shares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme.

The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments.

Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise £190m to bolster its finances.

Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year.

One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal".

Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

"Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve."

Capita said it was now expecting its underlying operating profit for 2027 to be hit by between £85m and £95m, having previously expected a reduction of up to £40m.

This comes from the extra cost of the recovery plan, as well the loss of two other "major" contracts in the defence and pension solutions divisions.

Capita said it was planning an equity raise of £190m in the first half of next year, in order for the company to "move forward from a more stable foundation".

The backlog of payments from the civil service pension scheme has been described as "hell" by people who have failed to receive money, some of whom retired early owing to ill health.

BBC Radio 4's Money Box programme has been hearing from people caught up in the saga, and left in financial hardship.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee of MPs, said: "The mishandling of the civil service pension scheme has caused severe hardship for some scheme members, particularly considerably delayed bereavement payments.

"The PAC will continue to pursue this dreadful matter and we can only hope that the new acting Chief Executive, Pablo Andres, will be able to get a grip on this whole affair."

articles.title: Catering giant Compass Group to shift main stock market listing to US in further blow to UK
articles.text:
Catering giant Compass Group is planning to switch its primary stock market listing from the UK to the US in a move which will deal another blow to the London Stock Exchange.

A source close to the company told the BBC an official announcement was expected to be made in its full-year results on Tuesday.

Compass Group is made up of several brands which supply food and drink to various places, ranging from football stadiums and visitor attractions to schools, universities and large corporations.

It is understood the proposed shift to the US, which was first reported by the Financial Times, external, is being made due to the number of investors and the increasing business Compass has across the Atlantic.

North America accounts for two-thirds of its business, which drove its total 2025 revenues to $46.1bn.

However, such a move would deal a further blow to the London Stock Exchange (LSE), which has seen a growing number of firms leave the UK to list shares in the US in recent years.

These include tech firm Arm Holdings, Just Eat, Deliveroo and Paddy Power's parent company Flutter.

Long-running speculation also remains over the future of London stalwarts Shell and pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca, which began listing shares in New York in February.

Compass describes itself as "possibly the biggest business you've never heard of" due to its plethora of catering and hospitality brands it operates its business under, which include Levy, Bon Appétit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells.
