articles.title: MotoGP: Is Marc Marquez, Valentino Rossi or Giacomo Agostini the sport's greatest of all time?
articles.text:
As Marc Marquez ascended a staircase, the silhouette of a goat matched his every step.

It was a nod to his increasing - or solidified, depending on who you ask - status as MotoGP's 'greatest of all time' (GOAT).

In winning the 2026 championship in Portugal on Sunday, Spain's Marquez secured his eighth overall title, the first per son in the modern era to achieve this accolade.

It drew the Ducati rider level with the great Giacomo Agostini, who won his eight titles between 1966-75.

And yet it is Valentino Rossi, who Marquez has now surpassed for World Championship crowns, who most view as his biggest rival for GOAT status.

"I feel proud when the fans and media say that I am one of the greatest of all time," Marquez told BBC Sport on Monday.

"I do not agree when they say I am the greatest because every athlete in motorsport has their moments, their career and injuries and I respect all of them, all the legends."

But despite his humility, is 33-year-old Marquez actually the sport's greatest? Have your say at the bottom of this article.

In winning his eighth premier class championship on Sunday, Marquez overcame the biggest points deficit in MotoGP history - 102 points - to take the title.

But Marquez is the ultimate comeback king.

Last year, he won his first title in six years, a period in which he overcame 109 crashes, multiple injuries including a broken arm, ankle, ribs and fingers, and a severe concussion.

In 2023 he told BBC Sport he was "not ready to win again" and at the end of that season finished 14th in the standings. He then left Honda, a team where he won six titles, to join Gresini Racing, the satellite Ducati team.

After a solid 2024 season, in which he claimed three feature race wins and two pole positions, he joined the factory Ducati team and now has two titles in two seasons with the Italian outfit.

But 2026 was not without its issues. Marquez was without a win when he arrived at the French Grand Prix in May, and things went from bad to worse after he suffered a crash in the sprint race at Le Mans and had to have operations on his foot and shoulder. He then missed the next round in Barcelona.

Marquez made his return at Mugello 20 days later, facing that hefty points deficit, to the then leader Marco Bezzecchi.

"In that moment after the crash in Le Mans and then the seventh surgery on the right shoulder, [my title charge] was completely over. I was in hospital. I was 102 points behind the leader and I was not the fastest rider on the track," said Marquez.

"Then I say OK you can believe in me, but if you are not the fastest you cannot recover points. Then I tried to be very focused, to work on the mental side and to understand where my level was. I accepted that the level was key during the season and I had to take points and wait for my moment."

Marquez then won seven of the next 13 grand prix races, twice missing out on the chance to seal the title in Qatar and Saturday's sprint race in the Algarve, before finally clinching the win with one race weekend to come in Valencia.

While Sunday marked his eighth MotoGP title, it was Marquez's 10th championship overall after wins in the 125cc and Moto2 categories on his journey to the top of the sport.

Let's look at the case for Rossi.

The Italian is a motorcycle racing legend and still has a cult like status around the world, even after retiring in 2021.

Rossi is a seven-time MotoGP champion, with nine world titles to his name.

The now 47-year-old remains the only rider in history to win World Championships in 125cc, 250cc, 500cc and MotoGP.

Rossi has a record 89 victories in the premier class but Marquez is closing the gap with 80.

Marquez is still the only rider to win a MotoGP championship in his rookie year and after that dominated the series, with six titles in seven seasons between 2013 and 2019.

He and Rossi do share some MotoGP history. They are the only two riders to have won at least two world titles with two different manufacturers.

The rivalry between Rossi and Marquez is legendary.

In 2013 their battle at the Corkscrew at Laguna Seca became infamous, with Marquez eventually taking the win.

The crashes have been dramatic too. In 2015 in Sepang, the pair collided with Marquez crashing out, resulting in a back-of-the-grid penalty for Rossi which ultimately cost him that year's title.

Rossi has continually claimed that his younger challenger deliberately sabotaged his championship hopes, admitting in a recent interview on Italian TV that "it still stings".

Two years later, in Argentina, the riders came to blows again, this time with Rossi hitting the tarmac.

At one time Rossi accused Marquez of "destroying" the sport, with Marquez stating their relationship was like a "divorce".

"It is a big pleasure to equal Giacomo Agostini in premier class titles," said Marquez.

"He is the greatest of all time."

But in the modern era, does Marquez have the edge?

With a contract at Ducati extended until 2028 you would not rule him out of winning more titles in the future, but for now, Marquez is revelling in the present.

"I want to enjoy the moment, this week," he said.

"I want to enjoy the next weekend in Valencia. That is a special weekend because it is in a Spanish city and [I will] celebrate the world championship there, and then we will have time to prepare for 2027."

articles.title: Afghan women with UK university offers 'heartbroken' after visas stopped
articles.text:
When Shahira Sadat received an invitation for a Chevening Scholarship interview, she felt a rare glimmer of hope.

The software engineer in Kabul had spent three years battling Taliban restrictions, jumping through hoops and working through power and internet outages to prepare her applications for UK universities and grants.

"I was so happy. I can't describe it because I allowed myself to dream about studying in the UK," she says.

But in March this year, the UK's Home Office announced an "emergency visa brake" on study visas for applicants from Cameroon, Myanmar, Sudan and Afghanistan. Skilled work visas for Afghans were also paused. It said the move was a response to widespread visa abuse and had been triggered by a sharp rise in asylum claims from these visa routes.

At the time, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she was "taking the unprecedented decision to refuse visas for those nationals seeking to exploit our generosity". The US barred all visas for Afghan nationals earlier in the year.

Sadat had three acceptance letters to study a masters in AI and machine learning from Sussex, Bradford and Northeastern University London. Now with a shot at getting funding from the UK government-funded Chevening scheme, she felt the education she'd been denied in Afghanistan was finally within reach.

Then came an email saying she would no longer be considered to study in the UK because she was from Afghanistan.

"It was really heartbreaking. I lost all my motivation. I cried for hours and hours," says Sadat, her eyes welling up with tears. "It was not just about education for me; it was the opportunity to resume my career and to build a future for myself."

In Afghanistan, diktats from the Taliban's supreme leader have severely restricted the lives of women. They cannot attend secondary schools or universities, and are barred from most forms of work.

In the western city of Herat, Alia - whose name we have changed - received a similar rejection to Sadat. Her offers to do a digital media masters in the UK were withdrawn, which she says left her feeling trapped.

"Everything is banned just because I am an Afghan woman," she says, her voice cracking with emotion.

In a highly competitive field of international students vying to get UK scholarships, Afghan women have additional challenges to navigate.

Alia had to attend a secret school to prepare for an English language test, in defiance of Taliban restrictions. Before long the institute was discovered and authorities shut it down - so she continued with an online teacher from Canada.

The next challenge was actually sitting the test. Most authorised test centres would not admit female students, Sadat says, in fear of falling foul of the regime's rules.

After that came the difficulty of finding a UK university willing to recognise a degree earned in Afghanistan.

Throughout the process, both Sadat and Alia say frequent power cuts disrupted their preparations. They also feared a repeat of the nationwide internet shutdown imposed by the Taliban's supreme leader in September 2025.

Many students also find it difficult to physically apply for the visas, as they often have to travel to neighbouring countries which are making it harder for Afghan nationals to enter.

Having overcome the obstacles, Alia finds the visa brake deeply disappointing: "I want to say to the UK government: don't treat us like our government. They have deprived us of education, so the global community should have more focus on us."

In response to the BBC's questions about the suspensions, the UK's Home Office pointed to the reopening of the UK Resettlement Scheme for refugees, "including Afghan women and girls". It also said it was introducing "named sponsorship and refugee study routes", which would give refugees "a safe pathway to come to the UK and rebuild their lives".

However, the Home Office did not answer specific questions about whether these routes would be open to women in Afghanistan who are not classified as refugees, such as Sadat and Alia, or how many places would be available to Afghans.

Data from the Higher Education Statistics Agency shows that fewer than 400 of the more than 680,000 international students in the UK in 2024-25 were from Afghanistan.

The Home Office did not respond to a question about how many of those students went on to apply for asylum, but previously said that between 2021 and September 2025, the number of Afghan asylum claims amounted to 95% of the study visas issued. It says its policy aims to address disproportionate levels of student asylum claims and ease pressure on the system.

We asked Zainab Rezaie, an Afghan student who moved to Birmingham in 2024 and later applied for asylum, why she made that choice.

Rezaie, who is pursuing a PhD in education at the University of Exeter, says she was "very anxious" about what would happen after she graduated. She feared that if her visa expired before she could secure a job or switch to another visa, she would have no choice but to return to Taliban-run Afghanistan where - especially given her field of studies - she would not be able to work, and the possibilities of her life would be severely limited.

Rezaie says she applied for asylum to "give myself some opportunity to think".

"The biggest contrast is that I'm not in prison in my room. I have the right to move around every day, to go out, to exercise, to buy something. Living in Western society, you may never think that the freedom to go out at any time is a big advantage. But in Afghanistan, every move women make has to be strategised."

She says it was "never my choice" to come and live in the UK as an asylum seeker. "It takes a lot of mental effort to live here on your own and to be separated from your family, to adjust to society… Nobody chooses this happily, willingly."

There are still opportunities for Afghans to study abroad, in Europe, Asia and elsewhere, but the women we spoke to fear other countries will follow in the US and UK's footsteps.

They feel the international community is slowly closing its doors on them.

Additional reporting by Imogen Anderson and Mahfouz Zubaide

articles.title: Trump faces backlash after he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over a reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company came under pressure by Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring him back.

But now both Trump and Nvidia are facing bipartisan backlash from lawmakers, just as Huang is due to testify before Congress next week.

The CEO's comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that left the S&P 500 in correction territory, and added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value.

Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.

But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.

As Asian stock markets opened, Nvidia racked up more gains and helped lift other share prices across the tech sector.

Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.

In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.

"Probably so," Trump said.

The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.

Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".

"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they got him back in," he says.

Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" and vowed that Congress will conduct "a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation".

"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said, echoing many lawmakers on Monday who said that Congress must pass strong export control legislation.

Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December. Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee once Democrats take control of the chamber in January, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".

"The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement," she also said.

Republicans, too, called for answers.

"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," said Republican Representative Don Bacon, who chairs a House subcommittee on cyber security.

"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."

The chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."

Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.

Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

The BBC has contacted the White House.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.

The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon and Rachel Clun

articles.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
articles.text:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.

The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.

Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.

That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potentially rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well as being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back".

Following the announcement of Huang's return, Musk posted: "The mistake has been corrected."

articles.title: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
articles.text:
It's being called a comeback for the ages.

For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.

Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.

Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.

So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?

Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.

The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.

Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.

They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".

But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.

Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.

But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by an announcement that Huang was stepping down.

He'd barely been gone, however, before a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign was launched, reportedly by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.

The man himself said he would be "honoured" to return, should the board ask him.

Although initially showing no interest in reinstating him, the board has now done just that, saying his return was "in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

articles.title: Next data accessed in cyber breach
articles.text:
Next has said that some of its data has been accessed in a cyber breach affecting a third-party online supplier.

The high street retailer said there was no evidence that customers' personal data had been compromised.

The firm - which has its headquarters in Enderby, Leicestershire - said it had been informed by one of its suppliers about the incident, which led to "unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next".

"We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier," the company told investors.

"Our investigations are ongoing. However, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised.

"The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next."

The company added it was treating the situation "with the utmost seriousness", and working with the supplier as well as the police and regulators.

Next is the latest retailer to be caught up in a cyber breach.

In October, Asos said an "unauthorised party" had gained access to an employee's account, leading customers to receive a phone alert saying that the retailer had been hacked.

The firm said the attacker gained access to some personal data, including names and contact details belonging to customers.

articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.text:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.

The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.

The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.

Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.

Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.

China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.

On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".

The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.

The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.

China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.

Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.

Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.

Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.

Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.

That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.

Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.

Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.

Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take.

The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.

In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.

Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title: GTA 6 hacker released on licence with warning 'don't let this happen again'
articles.text:
A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.

Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."

The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.

Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.

He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.

City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".

He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.

He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.

With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.

He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

articles.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.text:
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.

Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.

Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.

The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.

Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).

What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.

He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.

But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"

Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.

"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."

If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.

That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.

But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.

For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".

Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.

"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.

Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.

"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.

All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.title: Black Friday 2026: Can ChatGPT and other AI tools find you the best bargains?
articles.text:
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.

Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.

The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.

Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.

This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.

But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.

The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.

At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".

Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.

Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.

It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.

But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.

Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.

It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".

We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.

While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.

Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.

If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".

"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.

Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.

Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".

But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.

"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

articles.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
articles.text:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

Google has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
articles.text:
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired after losing the confidence of the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, according CBS, the BBC's US news partner. Asked about his removal on Friday, President Donald Trump said it was because he was not "good enough".

His firing comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.

US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.

There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.

The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.

Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".

But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.

articles.title: Beatles venue may not be allowed to play live music on rooftop
articles.text:
Plans to create a museum where The Beatles performed their last live performance is expected to be approved - but on condition no live music can be played on the rooftop that made the Mayfair venue famous.

Apple Corps Ltd, the company founded by the band, wants to convert 3 Savile Row into a seven-floor "cultural experience and exhibition" celebrating The Beatles, with a basement café-bar on the site of the studio where Let It Be was recorded in 1969.

The Beatles famously stunned locals in January 1969 by playing a set on the roof of the Grade II* listed building, which was Apple Corps' headquarters.

Westminster City councillors are due to vote on the plans on Tuesday.

The council papers set out for the first time the scale of the attraction Sir Paul McCartney announced in May.

Apple Corps is forecasting up to 900 visitors each weekday and 1,140 on weekends, entering in timed slots of 20 people every 10 minutes.

There is a proposed limit of 225 visitors at any one time.

The basement café/bar would open until midnight seven nights a week, and events would be capped at 104 a year, averaging two events a week.

The draft conditions also state that no live music can be played on the terrace and any amplified music or speech should be noise limited. A two-metre-high acoustic barrier has also been proposed.

articles.title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in single day - the biggest launch in history
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) saw record retail sales in its first full-day of release, hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history.

Take-Two, the parent company of Rockstar Games, said on Friday the figures were based on estimates through end of day on Thursday and marked a record for "entertainment across any medium". It pre-sold 32.5m copies of the game.

To compare, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, this year's highest-grossing film so far, made $2.5bn (£1.8bn) over its entire run in cinemas.

Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said earlier that PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch.

New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access.

In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times on the US East Coast.

In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany.

The record smashes that of its predecessor - from 13 years prior - Grand Theft Auto V. The game previously held the best opening week sales in video-game history, earning $1.15bn (£1.2bn) in just five days.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest release follows new characters, a pair of small-time criminals Lucia and her partner Jason.

articles.title: Don Toliver postpones London O2 arena show after Manchester evacuation
articles.text:
US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two shows in London this week, after his concert in Manchester on Sunday was evacuated when an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd.

Toliver was due to play The O2 on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday, but Live Nation said his "stage and production equipment remains in Manchester and cannot be moved in time".

One person was taken to hospital and 89 people showed "symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure" after Sunday's Co-op Live arena show, police said.

Fans described "distressing scenes" with people "choking", "screaming" and "coughing up blood" because of the effects of a substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.

The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December.

"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.

One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.

A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.

Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and "this gas coming out".

"It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".

There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."

Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.

Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat.

"[We] were just coughing and coughing... there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and... tears everywhere," she told the BBC.

Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing."

Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses.

"We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."

Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.

Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".

Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."

Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".

It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel "assured" about security measures.

"A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don't even know you've been checked," she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site.

Murray said that while the current technology is "good enough", it needed improvement over the next few years to become "more sophisticated".

Venues are currently focused on keeping out items – such as explosives – that could cause mass casualties, she added.

Jack, 21, said some people had "pink liquid" on them and they were taken off to be tested.

Charlie, 20, said he found the process a bit "invasive" and "confusing".

The friends said they were still suffering from symptoms, with a headache, chest pains and "really sore throat".

articles.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
articles.text:
Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.

A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.

Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.

Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.

In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.

The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.

Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.

The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.

Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.

articles.title: Russell Brand's wife says she'll honour prison rules after message row
articles.text:
The wife of disgraced comedian Russell Brand says she will "honour" the rules of his prison, a week after she read a message from her husband proclaiming his innocence.

Laura Brand, 39, drew criticism from ministers after reading out the message from inside HMP Littlehey last week, prompting the government to seek to have the episode removed from social media platforms.

She said on Sunday that she would continue to defend her family and herself over her portrayal in the media during the couple's weekly podcast, which she now presents alone.

Russell Brand, 51, is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"Last week's episode drew a considerable amount of attention," Laura Brand said during this week's episode of Sunday Service.

"Now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that."

In the relayed message last week, Russell Brand had said he was "not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for".

Laura Brand said she had spoken to him at the Cambridgeshire prison and said he was "OK".

Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

Further allegations have since been reported about him and some have called for consent laws to be revised.

His conviction has renewed conversation about safeguarding in the media industry, and whether some celebrities are still able to use their fame to prey on women and then silence them.

Ministers have pointed out that inmates are prohibited from making statements that are likely to cause their victims distress and have said Brand's message was being investigated.

A woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16, but who was not among the women whose accusations led to his conviction, said his prison message was "upsetting" and "really shocking".

The government attempted to have the podcast removed from YouTube, but this was refused by its owner Google. Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged social media companies to "show some decency and take these videos down".

On Sunday, Laura Brand also said that Sunday Service would be a place where she would "continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media's image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny".

She expressed feeling a mixture of "grief", "absence", "desolation" and "loneliness" since her husband's imprisonment.

articles.title: Paul Potts almost missed Britain's Got Talent audition because of Carphone Warehouse shift
articles.text:
Britain's Got Talent winner Paul Potts said he nearly missed his life-changing audition on the show because he had been unable to get time off from his job managing a phone shop.

The tenor shot to fame in 2007 after performing Nessun Dorma on the ITV talent show, but had unsuccessfully tried to change the date of his performance because of his shift at Port Talbot's Carphone Warehouse.

"It was only thanks to a colleague who normally didn't work Saturdays that came in to cover me - otherwise I wouldn't have been there," he said.

"So thanks Allison."

He has since released six albums, reached the final of America's Got Talent: The Champions and inspired the Hollywood film One Chance.

"I actually almost didn't end up going," he told BBC Radio Wales' My Welsh Life.

Almost 20 years later, as he prepares for a special homecoming concert in Port Talbot, Potts said he was honoured to be "still doing what I love doing".

"The only reason why I'm still doing that is because people still support me and I'll always be forever grateful for that."

Potts's homecoming, marking 20 years since his victory on Britain's Got Talent, will be in the newly refurbished Princess Royal Theatre, now renamed Yr Aelwyd.

articles.title: Strictly Come Dancing noise disruption prompts BBC apology
articles.text:
The BBC has apologised "for any offence caused" after lewd audio was heard during the live broadcast of Strictly Come Dancing.

A recording of sex noises appeared to be playing from the audience in Blackpool's Tower Ballroom as judge Motsi Mabuse gave feedback early in Saturday's episode. She paused before joking: "It's not me."

At the end of the programme, presenter Emma Willis apologised to viewers "if you heard any audio disruptions". A BBC spokesperson also issued an apology and said it was "investigating how this happened".

Lancashire police said it was assessing whether any criminal offences may have taken place, after receiving a formal complaint and a mobile phone being seized.

The moment was streamed on social media by content creator Daniel Jarvis, whose videos include pranks. He appeared to place a phone call before the audio began playing in the ballroom, and suggested he was trying to target judge Craig Revel Horwood for his "bullying".

Jarvis has previously claimed he was responsible for sex noises disrupting Match of the Day in 2023.

Willis told viewers: "Before we see the judges' leaderboard, we'd like to apologise if you heard any audio disruptions earlier in tonight's show and for any offence caused."

articles.title: Molly Meldrum: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend
articles.text:
King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.

Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.

The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.

Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.

Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.

Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.

"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.

Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.

He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".

On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."

Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.

"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."

"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."

Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

articles.title: ITV investigating Coronation Street actor Jacob Roberts after bar incident
articles.text:
ITV is investigating a Coronation Street actor following an alleged bar altercation.

Jacob Roberts is known for playing Det Con Kit Green on the ITV soap since 2024. According to reports by the Sun newspaper, video footage appears to show him shouting outside Kiely's Irish Bar in Manchester on 8 November.

Greater Manchester Police said officers had attended a bar in Watson Street at about 02:30 GMT following reports of a disturbance. No arrests have been made.

An ITV spokesperson said they were investigating and would be speaking with Roberts.

Roberts was allegedly trying to get into the bar, with staff claiming he was acting aggressively and swearing when he was told he could not come in as the venue was closing.

Roberts previously played Damon Kinsella on the Channel 4 soap Hollyoaks from 2017 until 2023, before joining the cobbles in 2024.

He has also appeared in Emmerdale and recently starred in the crossover episode Corridale.

His storylines on Coronation Street include being diagnosed with male breast cancer as well as fathering a child after an illicit affair with his girlfriend's daughter.

Roberts' representatives have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
articles.text:
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external

"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.

"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."

articles.title: Long-lost Chevalier landscape found in Maidenhead charity shop
articles.text:
A rediscovered 19th Century oil painting bought for £20 in a charity shop could be auctioned for up to £20,000.

Cape Schanck, Victoria, by Russian-Swiss artist Nicholas Chevalier, was discovered in a charity shop in Maidenhead, Berkshire.

It was brought to the attention of Adrian Biddell at London's Olympia Auctions, who established the painting was a Chevalier work that had been missing for 160 years.

"To find it now, quite unexpectedly, in a corner of the British high street, is an extraordinary find," he said.

The painting dates from 1862 and depicts the dramatic, rugged coastline at the southernmost tip of Australia's Mornington Peninsula, about 60 miles (96.5km) south of Melbourne.

The auction house said only two of five en plein air - meaning painted directly in front of the landscape it depicts - views of Cape Schanck by Chevalier that year were known to have survived until now.

Both are in the collection of the Art Gallery of New South Wales in Sydney.

It said the charity shop buyer had liked the landscape but had not been familiar with the artist or the painting's value.

Its appearance "resolves a longstanding gap in the documented history of Chevalier's work", it said.

It was leading Chevalier expert Simon Gregg who confirmed its whereabouts had previously been recorded as "unknown" in his catalogue of the artist's work.

"This was definitely painted en plein air," he said. "This was Chevalier's typical modus operandi."

Gregg added: "Most of the oil sketches have not survived, hence my delight that this one has shown up."

Biddell said Chevalier "was a remarkable visual talent, with an extraordinary ability to capture the drama, power and sheer scale of the natural world".

"The discovery of Cape Schanck, Victoria is hugely exciting," he said.

The painting will go under the hammer on 9 December.
